title: Intrabeam scattering of chirped electron bunches with non-Gaussian longitudinal distributions and slice mismatch
summary: Intrabeam scattering (IBS) can significantly increase the uncorrelated energy spread of high-brightness electron bunches in linear accelerators. For chirped bunches transported through beamlines with dispersion, however, the commonly used simulation codes elegant and RF-Track give substantially different predictions. To investigate this discrepancy, a semi-analytical slice model is developed for bunches with non-Gaussian longitudinal distributions and slice-dependent transverse mismatch. The model predicts slice energy-spread evolution in beamlines with dispersion and provides an independent reference for assessing the simulation results. Benchmarks in an achromatic arc show good agreement with RF-Track for both ideal Gaussian and realistic mismatched bunches in the tested cases. The proposed model provides a practical tool for evaluating IBS in linacs beyond the ideal-Gaussian approximation. The comparison also suggests directions for improving the accuracy and efficiency of PIC-based IBS simulations.

AI.tldr: A semi-analytical slice model is developed to resolve discrepancies between elegant and RF-Track predictions for intrabeam scattering in chirped electron bunches transported through dispersive beamlines; it predicts slice energy-spread evolution and agrees well with RF-Track in achromatic-arc benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Intrabeam scattering can significantly increase the uncorrelated energy spread of high-brightness electron bunches in linear accelerators, and for chirped bunches in dispersive beamlines the simulation codes elegant and RF-Track give substantially different predictions. An independent reference was needed to investigate this discrepancy.
AI.method: The paper develops a semi-analytical slice model for bunches with non-Gaussian longitudinal distributions and slice-dependent transverse mismatch. AI.result: The model shows good agreement with RF-Track for both ideal Gaussian and realistic mismatched bunches in the tested achromatic-arc cases. The abstract does not provide quantitative agreement metrics.

title: FCC-μe: High Energy, High Luminosity Muon-Electron Collider & Neutrino Factory at CERN
comment: To be published in $Acta~Phys. Pol. B$ - contribution to the proceedings of Workshop on "Ultra-cold Muons for the LHC", Sep 24-26, 2026, at AGH University of Kraków - 7 pages, 1 figure and 1 table
summary: The concept is presented of making at the FCC-$ee$ (or CEPC) facility $μ^+e^-$ collisions at the centre-of-mass energy between 1 and 2 TeV and the average luminosity above $10^{34}$cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, concurrently to the $e^+e^-$ collisions. First, a concise scientific motivation is given, including the exciting prospect of measurements of the Higgs boson self-interaction, and is followed by a presentation of the FCC-$μe$ layout -- from the source of ultra-cold anti-muons, through the muon booster, to the main muon ring. Basic considerations are also given regarding the machine-detector interface and the performance of the FCC-$μe$ and associated neutrino factory. The paper concludes with an outlook underlying relevance of such anti-muon beams for any future high energy storage ring as well as for neutrino science.

title: Bayesian optimization of longitudinally aligned CNT targets for 800 nm laser wakefield acceleration in the bubble regime
summary: Laser wakefield acceleration (LWFA) in solid-density plasmas can reach accelerating gradients in the TeV/m range, well above those of gaseous media, provided the driver is matched to the plasma. In nanostructured solids, this matching can be achieved by controlling the spacing between the nanostructures to reduce the effective density, enabling infrared pulses to excite wakefields in the bubble regime. Following numerical demonstrations with carbon nanotube (CNT) bundles on concentric cylindrical shells, a simpler, experimentally more accessible longitudinally aligned CNT (LA-CNT) target is investigated here, with the bundles on a triangular lattice within a square cross section and an optional central aperture. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations are coupled with Bayesian optimization to vary the effective density, target length, bundle radius and aperture radius for a fixed 100 mJ, few-cycle, 800 nm laser pulse, maximizing the laser-to-beam energy conversion efficiency for electrons above 20 MeV. With the aperture radius constrained to at least 0.5 $μ$m, the best target operates in the bubble regime and reaches an efficiency of 24.6%, delivering a 673 pC bunch with a mean energy of 36.6 MeV and a quasi-monoenergetic peak near 46 MeV, against 19% for the concentric-shell target under identical conditions. When the aperture is allowed to vanish, the optimization converges to denser and shorter targets, the efficiency peaks at 25.8%, and the best configurations deliver a higher charge at the cost of a lower peak energy and about 50% larger divergence; aperture-free targets among them retain a mean efficiency of 24.1%. The optimized targets are robust to random bundle displacements that preserve the effective density. By eliminating the need to pattern a micrometre-scale opening, aperture-free targets may facilitate proof-of-principle experiments on solid-state LWFA.

AI.tldr: The paper optimizes a longitudinally aligned carbon-nanotube target for solid-density laser wakefield acceleration using 3D particle-in-cell simulations and Bayesian optimization, achieving laser-to-beam energy conversion efficiencies of about 24–26% for electrons above 20 MeV with a fixed 100 mJ, few-cycle, 800 nm pulse.
AI.motivation: Solid-density plasmas can support TeV/m accelerating gradients if the driver is matched to the plasma. Nanostructured solids allow effective-density reduction by controlling nanostructure spacing, enabling infrared pulses to excite bubble-regime wakefields. The study aims to replace the previously demonstrated concentric cylindrical-shell carbon-nanotube target with a simpler, more experimentally accessible longitudinally aligned carbon-nanotube target.

The target consists of carbon-nanotube bundles on a triangular lattice within a square cross section, with an optional central aperture. The optimization objective is laser-to-beam energy conversion efficiency for electrons above 20 MeV.
AI.result: With the aperture radius constrained to at least 0.5 μm, the best target operates in the bubble regime and reaches 24.6% efficiency, producing a 673 pC bunch with 36.6 MeV mean energy and a quasi-monoenergetic peak near 46 MeV, compared with 19% for the concentric-shell target under identical conditions. Aperture-free targets eliminate the need to pattern a micrometre-scale opening and may therefore facilitate proof-of-principle experiments on solid-state laser wakefield acceleration.

title: Ionization and Dissociation Energies of Molecular Hydrogen
summary: Molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) is the simplest neutral molecule and its ionization and dissociation energies are key benchmarks for testing first-principles calculations of nonadiabatic, relativistic, quantum-electrodynamic and finite-nuclear-size effects in molecules. To obtain improved H$_2$ ionization and dissociation energies, we performed precision measurements of 15 transition frequencies in para-H$_2$. They connect the X $^1Σ_g^+(v=0,N=0)$ ground state, the long-lived EF $^1Σ_g^+(v=0,N=0)$ excited state, and several high members of the $n$p and $n$d Rydberg series with principal quantum number $n$ in the range between 48 and 70. The new data by itself leads to a five times more accurate value of the ionization energy of the ground state of para-H$_2$, equivalent to a relative frequency accuracy of $5\times 10^{-11}$. Combined with a global network analysis of 45 energy intervals in para- and ortho-H$_2$ that have been measured in the past three decades, we obtain new statistically robust values for the ionization energy [$E_{\rm I}(0,0)/(hc)= 124\,417.491\,1573(58)$~cm$^{-1}$] and the dissociation energy [$D_0^{N=0}=36\,118.069\,6646(58)$~cm$^{-1}$] of H$_2$. These values have an unprecedented accuracy equivalent to 175 kHz. The network analysis also leads to improved term values and dissociation energies of the excited states involved in the analysis. By comparing the results with first-principles calculations of the level structures of H$_2$ and H$_2^+$ , a significantly reduced upper bound of 540 kHz is derived for putative beyond-the-standard-model contributions to the energy difference between para- and ortho-H$_2$.

AI.tldr: Precision measurements of 15 para-H2 transitions were combined with a global network analysis of 45 para- and ortho-H2 energy intervals, yielding substantially improved ionization and dissociation energies and a reduced bound on beyond-standard-model para-ortho energy contributions.
AI.motivation: H2 is the simplest neutral molecule, and its ionization and dissociation energies are key benchmarks for first-principles calculations of nonadiabatic, relativistic, quantum-electrodynamic, and finite-nuclear-size effects in molecules. The study aims to improve these H2 values.
AI.method: The authors performed precision measurements of 15 transition frequencies in para-H2 connecting the X 1Sigma_g+(v=0,N=0) ground state, the long-lived EF 1Sigma_g+(v=0,N=0) excited state, and several high np and nd Rydberg states with principal quantum number n between 48 and 70. They combined the new data with a global network analysis of 45 energy intervals in para- and ortho-H2 measured over the past three decades.
AI.result: The new data alone give a five-times more accurate ground-state ionization energy of para-H2, with relative frequency accuracy of 5x10^-11. Combined with the network analysis, the results are E_I(0,0)/(hc)=124417.4911573(58) cm^-1 and D_0^(N=0)=36118.0696646(58) cm^-1, corresponding to an unprecedented accuracy equivalent to 175 kHz. The network analysis also improves term values and dissociation energies of the excited states involved, and comparison with first-principles calculations gives a reduced upper bound of 540 kHz for putative beyond-the-standard-model contributions to the para-ortho H2 energy difference.
AI.conclusion: The work provides highly accurate H2 ionization and dissociation energies, improved excited-state term values and dissociation energies, and a significantly reduced upper bound of 540 kHz for beyond-standard-model contributions to the para-ortho H2 energy difference.

title: High-Fidelity Universal Quantum Gates in a Cryogenic Atom Array
summary: Neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays have emerged as a leading platform for quantum information processing. The fidelity of entangling gates mediated by Rydberg interactions has improved rapidly and is increasingly constrained by blackbody-radiation-induced transitions, which shorten Rydberg lifetimes and create contaminant states that can cause correlated errors. Cryogenic environments can suppress these transition rates by more than an order of magnitude. However, realizing a universal gate set in such an environment has remained an outstanding challenge. Here, we demonstrate a universal quantum gate set in a cryogenic $^{133}$Cs atom array, with a single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.970(2)% and a raw two-qubit entangling-gate fidelity of 99.76(8)%, within the range of leading room-temperature implementations. The entangling gate uses direct single-photon coupling between the electronic ground state and a Rydberg $P$ state, avoiding scattering and light shifts associated with two-photon coupling. The gate operates at a modest Rabi frequency of $2π\times4.3$ MHz. The measured fidelity agrees with our error model dominated by atomic motion, indicating a straightforward route to higher fidelity through improved cooling, while the fundamental error contribution from Rydberg decay is below $3\times10^{-4}$. These results establish a path to entangling-gate fidelities substantially beyond the current state of the art through cryogenic suppression of Rydberg decay, reducing the overhead for fault-tolerant computation.

AI.motivation: Rydberg-mediated entangling-gate fidelity is increasingly limited by blackbody-radiation-induced transitions that shorten Rydberg lifetimes and create contaminant states causing correlated errors. Cryogenic environments can suppress these transition rates by more than an order of magnitude, but realizing a universal gate set in such an environment had remained an outstanding challenge.
AI.method: The authors implement a universal quantum gate set in a cryogenic 133Cs atom array. The entangling gate uses direct single-photon coupling between the electronic ground state and a Rydberg P state, avoiding scattering and light shifts associated with two-photon coupling, and operates at a Rabi frequency of 2π×4.3 MHz. Measured fidelity is compared with an error model.
AI.result: The single-qubit gate fidelity is 99.970(2)%, and the raw two-qubit entangling-gate fidelity is 99.76(8)%, within the range of leading room-temperature implementations. The measured fidelity agrees with an error model dominated by atomic motion, and the fundamental error contribution from Rydberg decay is below 3×10^-4.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a path to entangling-gate fidelities substantially beyond the current state of the art through cryogenic suppression of Rydberg decay, with improved cooling offering a straightforward route to higher fidelity and reduced overhead for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Simultaneous SI-traceable measurement of the amplitude and the ellipticity of microwave fields with cold Rydberg atoms
summary: We present a method for the simultaneous measurement of the amplitude and the ellipticity of microwave fields using trap-loss spectroscopy based on Rydberg excitation of a cold ensemble of 87Rb atoms. The measurement consists of probing the energy spectrum of the $61S_{1/2}$ to $61P_{1/2}$ transition in the presence of microwave, which depends on the electric field amplitude $|E|$ and the third Stokes parameter $|S_3|$. We use a millimeter-size magneto-optical trap to perform strongly-localized measurements, which mitigates the effect of microwave field inhomogeneities. This allows us to work with large Rabi frequencies and thus resolve small deviations from linear or circular states of polarization. Taking into account the effect of non-resonant couplings to neighboring Rydberg states, we measure $|E|$ and $|S_3|$ with an accuracy on the order of 1 percent in the Autler-Townes regime where the measurements can be traced to the international system of units. By studying the visibility of the spectral features as a function of the polarization of the excitation laser beams, we extract some information on the angle of arrival of the microwave field onto the atoms, with good agreement between theory and experiment.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates simultaneous measurement of microwave-field amplitude |E| and ellipticity via |S3| using Rydberg trap-loss spectroscopy in a cold 87Rb ensemble, achieving about 1% accuracy and extracting information on the microwave angle of arrival.
AI.motivation: The work aims to simultaneously determine microwave-field amplitude and polarization ellipticity while mitigating microwave inhomogeneities, resolving small deviations from linear or circular polarization, and enabling measurements traceable to the International System of Units.
AI.method: A millimeter-size magneto-optical trap provides strongly localized measurements on cold 87Rb atoms. Trap-loss spectroscopy probes the 61S1/2 to 61P1/2 Rydberg transition in the presence of microwaves; the spectrum depends on |E| and the third Stokes parameter |S3|. Non-resonant couplings to neighboring Rydberg states are included, and spectral-feature visibility is studied as a function of excitation-laser polarization.
AI.result: |E| and |S3| are measured with accuracy on the order of 1% in the Autler-Townes regime, where measurements can be traced to the International System of Units. Analysis of spectral-feature visibility yields information on the microwave angle of arrival onto the atoms, with good agreement between theory and experiment.
AI.conclusion: The method enables simultaneous, localized, SI-traceable measurement of microwave amplitude and ellipticity and can resolve small polarization deviations from linear or circular states; it also provides angle-of-arrival information. Specific angle values and further quantitative details are not provided in the abstract.

title: Theoretical Study of Classical Dynamics of Electron in Two-Frequency Paul Trap
summary: We present a theoretical study of trapping an electron in a two-frequency Paul trap, motivated by future hybrid architecture consisting of a doubly charged calcium ion (Ca$^{2+}$) and an electron. By isolating the electron from ionic-electron interactions, we formulate the equations of motion for the electron in the time-dependent trap potentials and cast them in the Hill form. Stability and dynamics are then analysed in terms of the dimensionless q-parameters, which encode the applied voltages, drive frequencies, trap geometry, and the particle's charge-to-mass ratio. Under the combined action of the two radio-frequency fields, the trapped electron's classical motion is shown to be approximated well by a slow secular oscillation modulated by two distinct motion sidebands originating from the low- and high-frequency RF drives. The approximation method presented here enables a quick evaluation of the relation between the device-design q-parameters and the electron motion. It offers a crucial foundation for developing physical models of electron-ion interactions in electron-ion traps.

AI.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows that an electron in a two-frequency Paul trap can be modeled via Hill equations and that its classical motion is a slow secular oscillation with two RF-drive sidebands, supporting future electron–ion trap models.
AI.motivation: The study is motivated by a future hybrid architecture combining a doubly charged calcium ion (Ca2+) and an electron; the electron is isolated from ionic-electron interactions for analysis.
AI.method: The authors formulate the electron equations of motion in time-dependent two-frequency trap potentials and cast them in Hill form. Stability and dynamics are analyzed using dimensionless q-parameters that encode applied voltages, drive frequencies, trap geometry, and charge-to-mass ratio, with an approximation method for the electron motion.

AI.conclusion: The work provides a crucial foundation for developing physical models of electron-ion interactions in electron-ion traps.

title: Light and charge yields from nuclear recoils in noble liquids: From sub-keV energies to 1 MeV
summary: We present a first-principles study of total quanta and charge recombination in noble liquids, based on a solution of Lindhard's integro-differential equation for atomic motion with electronic straggling and detailed modeling of inter-atomic potentials. We introduce the electronic scaling length $ξ_e$ as a fundamental parameter related to a physical observable of the system. We study the energy and electric-field dependence of the exciton-to-ion ratio for nuclear recoils based on the Bates-Griffing process and semiclassical atomic interactions. The resulting light and charge yields are expressed through the recombination probability in the Thomas-Imel box model using the calculated parameter $ξ_e$ and one fitted constant. We compare our model with recent measurements of the electric-field dependence of the box size in LAr and LXe and provide a physical explanation for this behavior. Our model extends to sub-keV energies and provides a consistent description of available data from a few keV to 1 MeV, yielding better overall agreement with existing LAr data than NEST and offering predictions for LXe.

AI.tldr: A first-principles model of total quanta and charge recombination in noble liquids uses Lindhard transport, detailed inter-atomic potentials, and a new electronic scaling length ξ_e to describe light and charge yields and Thomas–Imel box behavior from sub-keV to 1 MeV, with improved LAr agreement over NEST and predictions for LXe.
AI.motivation: To provide a physically grounded description of total quanta and charge recombination in noble liquids, including the energy and electric-field dependence of the exciton-to-ion ratio for nuclear recoils and the connection between recombination modeling and an observable system parameter in LAr and LXe.
AI.method: The study solves Lindhard's integro-differential equation for atomic motion with electronic straggling and detailed inter-atomic potentials, introduces the electronic scaling length ξ_e, models the exciton-to-ion ratio via the Bates-Griffing process and semiclassical atomic interactions, and expresses light and charge yields through the Thomas-Imel box-model recombination probability using calculated ξ_e and one fitted constant. It compares the model with measurements of electric-field-dependent box size in LAr and LXe.
AI.result: The model yields energy- and electric-field-dependent exciton-to-ion ratios and light/charge yields, reproduces the measured electric-field dependence of box size in LAr and LXe with a physical explanation, extends to sub-keV energies, consistently describes data from a few keV to 1 MeV, agrees better overall with existing LAr data than NEST, and provides LXe predictions. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the model provides a consistent first-principles-based description of recombination and light/charge yields in noble liquids, identifies ξ_e as a fundamental parameter related to a physical observable, and offers predictive capability for LXe; further numerical validation is not detailed in the abstract.

title: Extending the limits of rotationally resolved mid-IR spectroscopy: an accurate model of trioxane derived from combining Fourier transform and sub-Doppler measurements
summary: 1,3,5-Trioxane, a polyoxymethylene (POM) molecule relevant to prebiotic chemistry and astrophysics, exhibits a dense rovibrational spectrum that challenges high-resolution spectroscopic characterization. Here, we report an extensive study of its $ν$ 5 CO symmetric stretching mode (960-1000 cm -1 ) by combining broadband high-resolution FTIR spectroscopy (0.001 cm -1 resolution, >2000 transitions) with SI-traceable sub-Doppler saturated absorption measurements using frequency-stabilized CO 2 lasers and a frequency-comb-referenced quantum cascade laser. The latter achieve lineposition uncertainties as low as 40 kHz, revealing inaccuracies in the FTIR frequency scale. A frequency-scale correction is determined by maximizing the global consistency of the complete spectroscopic data set. A global least-squares Hamiltonian fit combining the calibrated FTIR data, the SI-traceable sub-Doppler measurements and previously reported millimeter-wave rotational transitions yields a refined spectroscopic model. The resulting analysis significantly improves the precision of the rotational, quartic, and sextic constants for both the ground and $ν$ 5 excited vibrational states. This work extends mid-infrared frequency metrology to the largest molecule studied to date (12 atoms), providing a dense set of reference transitions for frequency calibration around 970 cm -1 . The resulting spectroscopic parameters reach relative uncertainties as low as 3.7 x 10 -10 for the band origin, making them valuable for molecular databases used in astrophysics and atmospheric physics, as well as for precision measurements in fundamental physics. Additionally, the observed line shapes indicate the absence of significant intramolecular vibrational energy redistribution (IVR) within the investigated energy range, while a few discrepancies in the Hamiltonian fit suggest the onset of weak perturbations, demonstrating the sensitivity of the present approach to probe subtle intramolecular couplings in complex polyatomic spectra. title: Cold Hypersonic Gas Jets for Precision Laser Spectroscopy of Radioactive Molecules
summary: The sensitivity to possible beyond standard model physics via a study of the nuclear Schiff moment (NSM) has since recently been driving laser spectroscopy of short-lived radioactive molecules. These experiments have in part been hindered by inefficient cooling of the molecular degrees of freedom, resulting in complex, difficult to interpret molecular spectra. Hypersonic (de Laval) nozzles have been shown to provide ideal environments to study cold short-lived actinides by means of in-gas-jet laser ionization spectroscopy. We present here the first application of this technique on molecules using $^{229,230,232}$ThO laser ablation targets. Translational and rotational temperatures were characterized via laser spectroscopy and found to be $12.5(25)\,\mathrm{K}$ and $7.2(6)\,\mathrm{K}$, respectively, along the nozzle-collimated $60\,\mathrm{mm}$-long, $5\,\mathrm{mm}$-diameter gas jet. An upper bound of the vibrational temperature was estimated as no transitions from $v''=1$ were observed. Molecular King-plot analysis shows a large field shift of $-4.0(13)\,\mathrm{cm}^{-1}/\mathrm{fm}^2$, indicating enhanced sensitivity to the differential nuclear charge radii. Relativistic FSCCSD calculations reproduce the measured molecular field-shift factor, providing a benchmark between state-of-the-art molecular and atomic calculations.

AI.tldr: The first molecular application of in-gas-jet laser ionization spectroscopy with a hypersonic de Laval nozzle to laser-ablation-produced 229,230,232ThO characterized cold rotational and translational conditions, yielded a large molecular King-plot field shift indicating enhanced sensitivity to differential nuclear charge radii, and provided a benchmark between relativistic FSCCSD molecular calculations and atomic calculations.
AI.motivation: Sensitivity to possible beyond-standard-model physics through the nuclear Schiff moment has motivated laser spectroscopy of short-lived radioactive molecules, but inefficient cooling of molecular degrees of freedom has produced complex, difficult-to-interpret spectra. Hypersonic de Laval nozzles offer suitable cold environments for studying short-lived actinides via in-gas-jet laser ionization spectroscopy.
AI.method: The authors applied in-gas-jet laser ionization spectroscopy with a hypersonic de Laval nozzle to molecules for the first time, using 229,230,232ThO laser ablation targets. Laser spectroscopy was used to characterize translational and rotational temperatures along a nozzle-collimated 60 mm-long, 5 mm-diameter gas jet. Molecular King-plot analysis was performed, and relativistic FSCCSD calculations were compared with the measured molecular field-shift factor.
AI.result: Translational and rotational temperatures were measured as 12.5(25) K and 7.2(6) K, respectively. An upper bound on the vibrational temperature was estimated from the absence of observed transitions from v''=1; no numerical bound is provided in the abstract. King-plot analysis showed a large field shift of -4.0(13) cm^-1/fm^2, indicating enhanced sensitivity to differential nuclear charge radii. Relativistic FSCCSD calculations reproduced the measured molecular field-shift factor.
AI.conclusion: Hypersonic de Laval nozzle in-gas-jet laser ionization spectroscopy was successfully applied to ThO molecules, producing cold translational and rotational conditions, a large field-shift sensitivity, and agreement between relativistic FSCCSD calculations and measurement. This provides a benchmark between state-of-the-art molecular and atomic calculations and supports the technique's use for studying short-lived radioactive molecules relevant to nuclear Schiff moment sensitivity.

title: $3\times10^{-16}$ Stable Laser Deployed on a 4.3 km Mountain
summary: We present a transportable stable laser system based on a 10 cm reference cavity and an all-fiber phase-stabilized distribution network for the $^{171}$Yb clock wavelength. We highlight an extended cuboid cavity geometry with 4 times smaller spacer volume than a traditional cubic cavity of the same length [30]. We demonstrate repeatable acceleration sensitivities below $2\times10^{-10}$ g$^{-1}$ in all axes and fractional frequency instability as low as $3 \times 10^{-16}$. We also demonstrate accurate distribution of the stable light over 10 m fibers below the $1\times10^{-18}$ level in an all-fiber optic system. We report the successful deployment of the laser system to the summit of Mount Blue Sky at 4300 m, and for the first time, we report 16-digit laser instability measured outside the lab.

AI.tldr: A transportable 10 cm-cavity laser system at the 171Yb clock wavelength, with an all-fiber phase-stabilized distribution network, achieved low acceleration sensitivity and fractional frequency instability and was deployed to a 4300 m mountain summit, where 16-digit laser instability was measured outside the lab.
AI.motivation: The work targets a transportable stable laser system and all-fiber distribution at the 171Yb clock wavelength, including operation outside the laboratory and a more compact cavity geometry.
AI.method: The system uses a 10 cm reference cavity with an extended cuboid geometry having four times smaller spacer volume than a traditional cubic cavity of the same length, plus an all-fiber phase-stabilized distribution network. It was deployed to the summit of Mount Blue Sky at 4300 m.
AI.result: The authors report repeatable acceleration sensitivities below 2×10^-10 g^-1 in all axes, fractional frequency instability as low as 3×10^-16, and accurate distribution of stable light over 10 m fibers below the 1×10^-18 level in an all-fiber optic system. They also report successful deployment to Mount Blue Sky at 4300 m and, for the first time, 16-digit laser instability measured outside the lab.
AI.conclusion: The presented transportable laser system and all-fiber distribution network enable stable laser operation and accurate optical distribution outside the laboratory, as demonstrated by deployment to a 4300 m summit and the first outside-lab measurement of 16-digit laser instability.

title: Predicting Weight Windows for Duct-Streaming Shielding Geometries with a Convolutional Neural Network
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to M&C 2027, the International Conference on Mathematics and Computational Methods Applied to Nuclear Science and Engineering (American Nuclear Society)
summary: Forward-flux-based weight windows give global variance reduction for duct-streaming shielding problems, but each new geometry needs an iterative Monte Carlo calculation to build them. We report preliminary results on a convolutional neural network (CNN) that learns the map from a two-dimensional duct geometry and source position to the lower window bound of such an iteration, here the MAGIC generator in OpenMC, in milliseconds. A set of 250 random concrete ducts of three curved and rectangular families on the Protvino labyrinth bounding box was run in OpenMC with a Cf-252 point source and MAGIC generation, and a 1.9-million-parameter U-Net was trained on the logarithm of the lower bound. On held-out ducts the error in the cells that carry the flux is 0.14 to 0.51 decades; replicate MAGIC runs show this part of the map to be reproducible to a few hundredths of a decade, so the residual is model error, while below $10^{-6}$ the reference itself is noise. Applied without retraining to the rectangular Protvino labyrinth, the prediction correlates with MAGIC at 0.96. Used as weight windows there, with its deepest cells clamped at deployment, it gives an exit-detector figure of merit 54 times the analog value, 1.7 times that of the MAGIC generation run for the same geometry, and 0.80 of that of reused MAGIC windows whose construction it does not pay for. title: Exceptional Points as Witnesses of Non-Gaussian Noise
summary: Efficient control of quantum devices requires the knowledge of their environmental noise, yet the commonly measured power spectrum does not fully characterize non-Gaussian fluctuations of realistic environments. Here we show that exceptional points (EPs) in the noise-averaged dephasing response can expose observable signatures of non-Gaussian statistics, distinguishing environments with identical lower-order statistics. We also introduce a theoretical model that describes dephasing environments in terms of identical independent noise sources while preserving the power spectrum. Given a calibrated single-source model, the largest EP order extracted from the measured dephasing response determines the number of sources and predicts the higher-order statistics of the combined noise. We illustrate an atomtronic readout that maps distinct EP signatures onto an evolving ensemble-averaged atomic interference pattern. Our results connect non-Hermitian dynamics to environmental noise statistics, providing a route to characterize noise in quantum devices used in computing, metrology, and precision measurement.

AI.method: The authors show that EPs in the noise-averaged dephasing response can expose signatures of non-Gaussian statistics. They introduce a theoretical model describing dephasing environments as identical independent noise sources while preserving the power spectrum, and use the largest EP order extracted from the measured dephasing response to infer the number of sources and predict higher-order statistics given a calibrated single-source model. They also illustrate an atomtronic readout that maps EP signatures onto an evolving ensemble-averaged atomic interference pattern. Specific experimental parameters are not provided in the abstract.

title: ML-COHP: predicting bond descriptors using latent space of a universal interatomic potentials
summary: The integrated crystal orbital Hamilton population (ICOHP) is the standard measure of bond strength in a DFT calculation, but every structure needs its own DFT single point and LOBSTER projection, which takes days for a cell of a hundred atoms, such as a grain boundary or a catalytic nanoparticle. We predict ICOHP from the frozen descriptors of a MACE foundation model. A symmetric pair head reads the scalar and bond-projected vector channels of the two atoms and corrects a pair baseline built from the element embeddings of the same model. We tested the model on the high-entropy diboride (Hf,Zr,Ti,Nb,Ta)B$_2$, Pt clusters on defective graphene and Pt/Pd nanoparticles with adsorbed O$_2$. The error on bonds stronger than 0.5 eV is 1.6-4.1%, about half that of the Gaussian-process model of Ferreira et al. trained on the same data. Trained only on high-temperature HEB$_2$ snapshots, the model reproduces the LOBSTER ICOHP of relaxed grain boundary cells to 0.06 eV in about a second, against 5-51 hours of LOBSTER. The vector channels halve the error compared to the scalar ones, and the baseline keeps the model usable with two training structures. With geometries from a fine-tuned MACE potential, the model gives the bonding of Pt/Pd particles over a continuous O$_2$ coverage, and DFT on these particles shows that O$_2$ costs a Pt-rich shell several times more metal--metal bonding than a Pd shell.

AI.method: Frozen descriptors from a MACE foundation model feed a symmetric pair head that reads the scalar and bond-projected vector channels of the two atoms and corrects a pair baseline built from the same model's element embeddings. AI.conclusion: Frozen MACE descriptors with a symmetric pair head enable fast and accurate ICOHP prediction for large and complex systems, supporting scalable bond-strength analysis and adsorption studies; vector channels and the element-embedding baseline improve accuracy and data efficiency.

title: Static dipolar impurity in a Fermi gas
summary: We consider a static dipolar impurity immersed in a Fermi gas and show how dipolar interactions shape both the few-body scattering properties and the resulting polaron physics. Using Fumi's theorem, we connect the anisotropic phase shifts directly to the ground-state energy, and compute the exact impurity spectrum via the functional determinant approach. The resulting spectrum is a convolution of independent even- and odd-wave contributions, giving rise to a ground state with simultaneously occupied even- and odd-wave bound states whose separation is tunable via the dipole length. A variational ansatz limited to one particle-hole excitation fails to capture this doubly occupied ground state. We further find that long-range dipolar interactions weaken Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe, reducing the power-law decay of the quasiparticle weight. These effects can be tested with ultracold polar molecules, where microwave shielding and independent tunability of interactions enable experimental access to the predicted regimes.

The exact impurity spectrum is a convolution of even- and odd-wave contributions, produces a doubly occupied bound-state ground state tunable by the dipole length, and shows weakened Anderson orthogonality catastrophe, with experimental relevance for ultracold polar molecules.

They also assess a variational ansatz restricted to one particle-hole excitation and discuss experimental access via microwave shielding and independently tunable interactions in ultracold polar molecules.

The ground state simultaneously occupies even- and odd-wave bound states, with their separation tunable via the dipole length. Long-range dipolar interactions weaken Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe and reduce the power-law decay of the quasiparticle weight.
AI.conclusion: Dipolar interactions qualitatively alter the impurity spectrum, bound-state occupancy, and orthogonality-catastrophe behavior. These effects are predicted to be experimentally accessible with ultracold polar molecules using microwave shielding and independent interaction tunability.

title: A Gaussian-Process Surrogate for Control Rod Worth with Calibrated Uncertainty: Application to VERA Core Physics Benchmark Problem 4
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to M&C 2027, the International Conference on Mathematics and Computational Methods Applied to Nuclear Science and Engineering (American Nuclear Society), 2 October 2026
summary: Differential and integral control rod worth are usually obtained by differencing eigenvalue calculations at discrete rod positions, which resolves the derivative poorly and gives it no uncertainty. A parametric sigmoidal mean carries the dynamic range, a Matern-5/2 GP carries the residual, and the reported Monte Carlo uncertainty of each run enters as known observation noise. Because differentiation is linear, the differential rod worth and its variance follow in closed form from the kernel derivatives. Trained on 43 runs at three particle counts and tested on 11 independent runs, the surrogate meets a fixed 10 pcm accuracy target above the test-run noise, and its intervals are calibrated: the standardized leave-one-out residuals over 129 independent runs have variance 1.07 with 95% interval [0.85, 1.39]. The total worth agrees with the direct OpenMC end-point difference within combined uncertainty, and the differential worth peak is located to within one step. Three mean functions of very different fit quality give the same differential worth to within 0.1 pcm/step, while the width of its band depends on the kernel smoothness by a factor of four. The number of runs required and the remaining approximations are reported, and the extension to rod position and soluble boron is outlined.

title: On the closure of 2D flamelet theory in non-orthogonal composition spaces
summary: Formal relations between scalar dissipation rates and curvatures are developed in the context of non-orthogonal two-dimensional composition spaces. These show that it is possible to achieve general closure of flamelet theory in terms of strain rates only, but that this requires the consideration of at least three different parameters (both in non-orthogonal and orthogonal spaces).

AI.tldr: The paper derives formal links between scalar dissipation rates and curvatures in non-orthogonal two-dimensional composition spaces and finds that flamelet theory can be generally closed using strain rates only, provided at least three parameters are considered.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not explicitly state the motivation, but the work targets general closure of flamelet theory through relations between scalar dissipation rates and curvatures.
AI.method: Formal relations between scalar dissipation rates and curvatures are developed in the context of non-orthogonal two-dimensional composition spaces.
AI.result: The relations show that general closure of flamelet theory in terms of strain rates only is possible, but it requires at least three different parameters, both in non-orthogonal and orthogonal spaces.
AI.conclusion: Closure of flamelet theory using strain rates alone is feasible, but not with fewer than three distinct parameters; this requirement applies in both non-orthogonal and orthogonal composition-space formulations.

title: Single-atom billiards in an ultracold bath with energy-tunable collisions and threshold-sensitive detection
summary: Transport processes at the microscopic scale can differ strongly from their macroscopic counterparts, particularly when the environment is not a well-defined surface but an unordered thermal medium. Ultracold quantum gases offer a high degree of controllability and directly observable dynamics, thereby providing a versatile platform to study such transport processes under precisely controllable conditions. Here, we realize an energy-tunable single-atom collider by transporting individual cesium atoms at controlled velocity through an ultracold rubidium bath. The constant lattice velocity sets the directed contribution to the collision-energy distribution, while the lattice depth provides a tunable energy threshold for collision-induced transport disruption. By independently varying these parameters together with bath density and temperature, we separate the number of collision events from their probability to disrupt transport. Across a regime with only a few expected collisions per passage, the inferred single-collision ejection probability rises from small values to near unity as the collision energy exceeds the lattice confinement scale. The experiment thus converts microscopic collisional energy transfer into a binary single-atom observable and provides a controlled link between individual scattering events and emergent dissipative transport.

AI.tldr: The authors use an ultracold cesium–rubidium mixture to build an energy-tunable single-atom collider and show that the probability of a single collision ejecting a transported atom rises from small values to near unity when the collision energy exceeds the lattice confinement scale.
AI.motivation: Microscopic transport in unordered thermal media can differ strongly from macroscopic transport, and ultracold quantum gases provide a controllable, directly observable platform for studying such processes.
AI.method: Individual cesium atoms are transported at controlled velocity through an ultracold rubidium bath using a lattice. Lattice velocity sets the directed collision-energy contribution, lattice depth sets an energy threshold for collision-induced transport disruption, and bath density and temperature are varied independently to separate the number of collision events from their probability of disrupting transport.

AI.conclusion: The experiment maps microscopic collisional energy transfer onto a binary single-atom observable, providing a controlled link between individual scattering events and emergent dissipative transport.

title: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh: GPU-Native Meshes and Simulation Cases for Physics AI
summary: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh is the mesh module of the open-source PhysicsNeMo library. It provides mesh processing similar to PyVista, but on the GPU, in batches, and inside PyTorch's automatic differentiation. Like xarray for unstructured meshes, it attaches semantics to data: fields on points, cells, and whole meshes have names and shapes, and a simulation case keeps the complete PDE problem specification, including boundary conditions and their prescribed values. It addresses three problems that plague machine learning for physical simulation. First, GPU utilization is bottlenecked by I/O, because samples are very large relative to the compute per forward pass. Second, because traditional preprocessing is expensive, it is necessarily done once, during curation, rather than differently for each model and workflow at the point of use. Finally, advanced equivariant and mesh-native architectures require information that curation ordinarily discards. Fast GPU mesh processing makes it practical to preprocess at the point of use: on one GB200 GPU, mesh operations run $6.2\text{--}1{,}068\times$ faster than VTK with 72 threads, and loading a whole case is $8.0\text{--}88\times$ faster than reading its VTK files ($8.0\times$ when both read the same fields). Overlapped with training, this preprocessing costs $2.1\%$ of throughput for a $127\,\text{ms}$ Transolver step. So one dataset serves many models and workflows: in PhysicsNeMo's public recipe, one stored DrivAerML dataset feeds Transolver, GeoTransolver, and GLOBE. PhysicsNeMo-Mesh combines the speed of an intermediate array store with the flexibility of an archival format such as VTK. When shapes and wall conditions both vary, per-boundary conditions cut a heat-conduction error from $87\%$ to $6\text{--}9\%$. And by keeping field ranks and named boundaries, it retains the semantic structure that next-generation architectures will need.

AI.tldr: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh is a GPU-native, batched mesh-processing module for PyTorch that adds semantic named fields and complete simulation-case specifications. It enables point-of-use preprocessing by accelerating mesh operations and case loading far beyond VTK, with small throughput overhead when overlapped with training, allowing one dataset to serve multiple models while preserving boundary and field semantics needed by advanced architectures.

title: Aerodynamic Shape Optimization of unsteady flapping wings
summary: This study introduces a new approach for building surrogate models, in the form of Reduced Order Models (ROMs), for PDE-constrained optimization. A physics-constrained data-driven framework is developed to transform large-scale non-linear optimization problems into ROM-constrained optimization problems. Unlike conventional methods, which suffer from instability of the forward sensitivity function, the proposed approach projects optimization problems to system dynamics optimization problems in Hilbert space to increase stability, diminish memory requirements, and lower computational cost. The present approach is applied to shape optimization of a 2D flapping wing section at $Re=2,400$, where the non-linear interaction of the wing with fluid includes chaotic flow structures. It is shown that the proposed approach can significantly enhance the time-averaged thrust force and propulsive efficiency by 37\% and 40\%, respectively. We also tested this approach for a 3D flapping wing and the results reveal the potential of the proposed approach for more complex optimal designs in the aerospace industry.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a physics-constrained, data-driven reduced-order modeling framework for PDE-constrained optimization that reformulates large-scale nonlinear problems as ROM-constrained optimization problems in Hilbert space. Applied to a 2D flapping wing section at Re=2400 with chaotic fluid structures, it improves time-averaged thrust and propulsive efficiency by 37% and 40%, respectively; a 3D flapping-wing test indicates potential for more complex aerospace designs.
AI.motivation: Conventional PDE-constrained optimization methods can suffer from instability of the forward sensitivity function, as well as high memory requirements and computational cost for large-scale nonlinear problems. The paper aims to address these limitations through stable, efficient surrogate ROM-based optimization.
AI.method: The authors develop a physics-constrained data-driven framework that builds Reduced Order Models and transforms large-scale nonlinear optimization problems into ROM-constrained optimization problems. The optimization problems are projected to system dynamics optimization problems in Hilbert space to increase stability, reduce memory requirements, and lower computational cost. The approach is applied to shape optimization of a 2D flapping wing section at Re=2400, where the nonlinear wing-fluid interaction includes chaotic flow structures, and is also tested on a 3D flapping wing.
AI.result: For the 2D flapping wing section, the proposed approach significantly enhances the time-averaged thrust force by 37% and propulsive efficiency by 40%. The 3D flapping-wing test results indicate the approach's potential for more complex optimal designs in the aerospace industry. Specific quantitative 3D results are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed physics-constrained data-driven ROM approach can stabilize PDE-constrained optimization by working in Hilbert space, reduce memory requirements and computational cost, substantially improve flapping-wing thrust and propulsive efficiency in the 2D case, and shows potential for complex 3D aerospace optimal design problems.

title: Resolving Photochemical Reaction Pathways Using Field-Induced Surface Hopping Simulation of fs-EUV-TRPES: The Case of Furan
summary: Recent advances in femtosecond extreme ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy have enabled insight into photochemistry in gases, condensed phases, and at interfaces. Assigning spectral features to reaction pathways requires theoretical predictions connecting nonadiabatic dynamics to measured observables. Here, we present a general approach for resolving photochemical reaction pathways by combining field-induced surface hopping with explicit pulse excitation, RMS-CASPT2, and simulations of time-resolved photoelectron spectra. The pump field prepares the excited-state ensemble under experimental conditions, while the multireference treatment describes excited states, conical intersections, and bond-breaking coordinates. Mapping trajectories onto photoelectron signals, supported by a systematic analysis of photoionization approximations, enables comparison with experiment. We apply this approach to furan excited by a 200 nm, 10 fs pulse. Among trajectories returning to the ground state, approximately 87 % hop near the ring-puckering conical intersection and 13 % near the ring-opening intersection. Subsequent ground-state vibrational energy redistribution nevertheless populates ring-opening structures. Five ground-state products are identified. Simulated spectra reproduce time-dependent electron-binding-energy shifts, characteristic kinks, and bands with predicted photoproduct contributions. Compared with Dyson-norm-based intensities, plane- and Coulomb-wave continuum functions improve the early-time shape of the lowest binding energy signal and show that photoelectron anisotropy is more sensitive to the continuum approximation than the angle-integrated spectrum. More generally, these findings demonstrate how explicit-pulse nonadiabatic dynamics and dynamically correlated multireference electronic structure can resolve competing photochemical reaction pathways through simulated fs-EUV-TRPES.

title: Dual Area-Volume-of-Fluid (DAVOF): co-advecting volume and face-area fractions for a closed-form, cell-local interface normal and position on unstructured meshes
comment: 45 pages, 9 figures, 18 tables. Code: https://github.com/tmaric/TwoPhaseFlow (branch davof) and https://github.com/leia-openfoam/leia (branch development)
summary: Geometric Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) on unstructured polyhedral meshes reconstructs the interface orientation from the volume fractions of a stencil of neighbours; on irregular cells and in the presence of wisps it degrades, and the curvature built on it drives the parasitic currents of capillary flows. We transport, consistently to the volume fraction of every cell, the wetted fraction of every face area. From the area and volume fractions, closed-form equations recover the interface normal and position of a cell, for the first time in VOF: the normal from one sum over the cell's own faces, the divergence theorem on the liquid sub-volume, and the plane's position from a second, without neighbours or iteration. Both identities are exact for a plane on hexahedral, perturbed and polyhedral cells. On a sphere and an ellipsoid the normal has the order of the face fractions, the position is second order for every state and mesh, and a quadric through one ring of recovered normals gives a converging curvature where the reference models show none. Transported with the plane clipping, the ring normal, the same identity on the union of the cell's ring, stabilises the state and carries a sphere over 3.3 diameters bounded and conservative, first order in the face fractions as the clipping law predicts, at plicRDF's position and shape errors. A preliminary transport implementation with one paraboloid per cell, its frame from the normal, its curvature tensor from the ring and its position from the volume fraction, carries the sphere bounded and conservative over the resolution ladder with face fractions of order 2.8 per period with the exact normal and 2.1 with the ring quadric's normal over N = 32 to 128. The loop has the order of the normal it is fed; a transported normal of second order is the research goal. This document is the basis on which the further development of the method is documented.

AI.tldr: A geometric VOF method for unstructured polyhedral meshes transports face wetted-area fractions together with cell volume fractions and uses closed-form divergence-theorem identities over a cell's own faces to recover the interface normal and position without neighbour stencils or iteration; tests show exact planar recovery, improved curvature, and bounded conservative sphere transport, while a second-order transported normal remains the goal.
AI.motivation: Geometric VOF normally reconstructs interface orientation from the volume fractions of a stencil of neighbours, which degrades on irregular cells and in the presence of wisps; the curvature built on this reconstruction drives parasitic currents in capillary flows.
AI.method: For every cell, the wetted fraction of each face area is transported consistently with the cell volume fraction. Closed-form equations then recover the interface normal from one sum over the cell's own faces via the divergence theorem on the liquid sub-volume, and the plane position from a second identity, without neighbours or iteration. Plane clipping is used for transport; a ring normal applies the same identity to the union of the cell's ring, and a preliminary paraboloid-per-cell transport uses the normal for its frame, a ring-derived curvature tensor, and the volume fraction for position.
AI.result: The identities are exact for a plane on hexahedral, perturbed and polyhedral cells. On sphere and ellipsoid tests the normal is of the order of the face fractions and position is second order for every state and mesh; a quadric through one ring of recovered normals gives converging curvature where reference models show none. With plane clipping and the ring normal, a sphere is carried over 3.3 diameters bounded and conservative, first order in face fractions as the clipping law predicts, at plicRDF's position and shape errors. The preliminary paraboloid transport keeps the sphere bounded and conservative over the resolution ladder, with face fractions of order 2.8 per period using the exact normal and 2.1 using the ring-quadric normal for N = 32 to 128.
AI.conclusion: The method provides closed-form, stencil-free normal and position recovery from transported face and volume fractions, stabilises transport and yields conservative sphere advection; its accuracy is limited by the order of the normal supplied, and a second-order transported normal is the stated research goal. The abstract does not provide a second-order transported normal or a full comparative benchmark beyond plicRDF.

title: Wave Turbulence of Capillary Waves in Finite Systems
summary: We consider classical problem of turbulence of capillary waves. In a series of numerical simulations it is shown that Zakharov-Filonenko spectrum corresponding to direct cascade of energy has a limited dynamic range of realization in a finite system, which shrinks with decreasing level of nonlinearity. Recent hypothesis that this dynamic range scales with average steepness as $\simμ^{8/3}$ is confirmed. As a byproduct the Zakharov-Filonenko spectrum was observed for record dynamic range close to or beyond one decade in a variety of simulation configurations.

AI.tldr: Numerical simulations of capillary-wave turbulence confirm that the Zakharov-Filonenko direct-cascade spectrum has a finite-system dynamic range that decreases with nonlinearity and scales with mean steepness as ∼μ^{8/3}; record ranges near or above one decade were observed.

title: Exploring Fractional Quantum Hall States with Deep Learning: From Abelian to Non-Abelian Phases

title: Simulation of non-stationary anisotropic capillary wave turbulence within the framework of the kinetic equation
summary: In the present work, numerical simulation of the evolution of capillary turbulence was performed on the basis of the wave kinetic equation taking into account energy dissipation at small scales. title: On the gauge-invariant orbital angular momentum of vector optical vortices in the paraxial approximation and beyond
summary: In this paper we present a gauge-invariant formalism for describing the spin and orbital angular momenta of scalar and vector optical vortices. title: Optical clock network tracks tidal variations of the gravity potential
summary: Gravity affects the passage of time, as described by General Relativity. On Earth, the rate of a clock as seen by a fixed observer changes by about one part in $10^{16}$ per metre in height. Chronometric levelling exploits this effect to directly measure differences in gravity potential by comparing distant clocks. Yet, the potentials of the Moon, the Sun and other celestial bodies as well as the Earth's response to their tidal forcing change clock rates by several $10^{-17}$, providing a predictable test signal to demonstrate optical clock networks resolving small variations in relativistic time dilation. Here, we report chronometric observations of time-varying gravity potential differences using a network of optical clocks and phase-stabilized fibre links in Europe. Two distinct geographical configurations, with baselines of about 800 km each, result in different combinations of diurnal and semidiurnal tidal components. One comparison uses a transportable optical clock as a remote sensor. The measured rate shifts track the tidal variations, resolving the predicted signal within 1 d of measurement and agreeing with model predictions. These results extend experimental chronometric levelling from static to dynamic potential differences and highlight the need to account for the time dependence of relativistic time dilation in frequency metrology. They also open the prospect for quantum clock networks with improved stability and availability to move beyond known tides and monitor other gravity potential variations, such as those arising from surface deformation and mass redistribution in geologically or volcanically active regions.

title: Generalizing Density Functional Theory with a Particle-Hole Expansion
summary: Strong electron correlation remains difficult to describe within conventional density functional approximations, particularly when natural-orbital occupations become strongly fractional. title: Critical-level wave absorption controls chaos in a wave--mean flow system
summary: Wave-mean flow interactions in stratified fluids can drive spontaneous oscillations, yet the mechanisms controlling transitions between periodic and chaotic regimes remain poorly understood. title: Nonlinear Jackiw-Rebbi exciton-polaritons at van der Waals topological interfaces
comment: 25 pages, 5 main-text figures; includes Supplementary Information
summary: Topological photonic structures provide a powerful means of confining and directing light through interface states formed between photonic phases with distinct topological properties. Van der Waals (vdW) materials offer complementary opportunities for nanophotonics: their optical properties can be selected from a wide family of layered crystals, while their atomically smooth surfaces and lack of lattice-matching constraints enable complex photonic heterostructures to be assembled layer by layer. Here, patterned low-loss dielectric hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) defines the photonic modes, while an encapsulated WSe2 monolayer provides the excitonic resonance that couples directly to the confined optical field. Strong coupling between the WSe2 exciton and a photonic Jackiw-Rebbi state localised at the interface between two topologically distinct gratings produces upper and lower Jackiw-Rebbi polariton branches. By varying the temperature from 4.7 to 300 K, we tune the exciton across the photonic bandgap and trace the evolution and anticrossing of these branches using angle-resolved reflectance and photoluminescence spectroscopy. title: Reverse Quantum Annealing for Ground-State Energy Calculation in Molecule
summary: We present the results of our reverse quantum annealing computations of the ground-state energies of alkaline-earth monofluoride molecules. title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
comment: 84 pages, 19 figures, 3 tables. Code: https://github.com/srikrrish/operator_learning (tags neopic-arxiv-v1, neopic-arxiv-v1-nufft); analysis scripts: https://github.com/NEOPIC-framework/neopic-paper-scripts
summary: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. title: On the rise of a Taylor bubble-drop assembly in a vertical tube

title: Temporal equivalent of the Sommerfeld half-plane problem

In addition, we observe the excitation of additional electric and magnetic field waves generated by a "DC" current density associated with the time interface. Our findings offer insight into the electromagnetic wave behavior at temporal transitions in dispersive media and may find applications in time- and space-time metamaterials

title: A semi-implicit unified gas-kinetic wave-particle method with energy-conserving electromagnetic coupling for multiscale plasmas
summary: In multiscale plasmas, kinetic regions coexist with collision-dominated, strongly magnetized and quasi-neutral ones. In these regions, the collision time, the cyclotron period and the plasma period, respectively, are far shorter than the flow time scales. Schemes that treat the collisions and the field coupling explicitly must take time steps below these times and below the light-crossing time of a cell. This paper presents a semi-implicit unified gas-kinetic wave-particle (UGKWP) method for the multispecies Vlasov-Maxwell system with Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook collisions. The electric field follows from a reformulated Maxwell equation, a single linear system with a unique solution for any time step. Its current response is built from the implicit-midpoint velocity map, which then pushes the particles and the hydrodynamic wave alike. The field step conserves the discrete total energy exactly and remains stable without resolving the cyclotron period, the plasma period or the light-crossing time, so that the time step follows from the flow and sound speeds. A Gauss's law correction adjusts the electric field and the joint charge of particles and wave while conserving the mass, momentum and energy of every charged species. The method reproduces whistler waves and electron plasma waves from Landau damping to collision-dominated oscillations. It agrees with particle-in-cell, two-fluid and magnetohydrodynamic references in a Brio-Wu problem from weak to strong collisionality and magnetization, the Orszag-Tang vortex and collisionless magnetic reconnection. It needs far less CPU time than either the UGKWP method with an explicit solver for the perfectly hyperbolic Maxwell equations or a deterministic multiscale kinetic scheme. In collisional plasmas, it also needs less CPU time than an implicit particle-in-cell method with the same collision operator, increasingly so as collisions strengthen.

It is validated on waves and standard plasma problems and is computationally cheaper than several reference methods.

The electric field is obtained from a reformulated Maxwell equation forming a single linear system with a unique solution for any time step. The field step exactly conserves discrete total energy and is stable without resolving the cyclotron period, plasma period, or light-crossing time, allowing the time step to follow flow and sound speeds. A Gauss's law correction adjusts the electric field and the joint charge of particles and wave while conserving each charged species' mass, momentum, and energy.

title: Gravitational Interactions in Nuclear Clocks
summary: Atomic clocks achieve extraordinary precision through quantum control over large ensembles of atoms, with precision increasing and atom number advancing steadily. Emerging nuclear clock technology encodes clock states in nuclear rather than electronic transitions, offering a new frontier for precision measurement. Here we study whether a large ensemble of such clock nuclei could be used to observe their mutual gravitational interaction. We investigate the gravitational redshift induced by neighboring atoms, including nuclear energy superpositions as sources of gravity, giving rise to a genuinely quantum gravitational interaction between pairs of nuclei. We find that the resulting clock frequency shift due to mutual gravity may become non-negligible for a macroscopic number of nuclei, for instance in a solid-state thorium clock, and we propose approaches to mitigate electromagnetic field effects by exploiting spatial symmetry and high-precision spectroscopy. We further discuss how energy-induced mass superpositions could be directly probed using external gravitational field sensors. By contrast, observing gravity-induced entanglement involving clocks would require substantially greater experimental advances due to decoherence from spontaneous emission. Taken together, our results suggest that nuclear clocks, either alone or in combination with complementary sensors such as optomechanical systems, may offer a future route toward probing gravity at short distances and testing gravitating quantum source masses beyond the Newtonian limit.

title: Single-Temperature Ranked Greedy Cluster Exchange for Max-Cut on Two-Dimensional Tori
summary: Ground-state search in two-dimensional Ising spin glasses on large toroidal lattices remains challenging for local-update heuristics because rugged energy barriers impede relaxation across metastable states. Equivalent to zero-field toroidal Max-Cut problems, these spin-glass instances also serve as standard benchmarks for optimization heuristics. Many Monte Carlo approaches combine single-spin flips or cluster moves with temperature ladders or annealing schedules, yet even with tuned parameters, rarely achieve rapid, reliable ground-state convergence at scale. Here, we address the need for faster ground-state search through cooperation between replicas. We introduce ranked greedy cluster exchange (RGCX) and combine it with fixed-temperature Metropolis sweeps to form single-temperature RGCX. Replicas are ranked by cut to determine the pair-processing order. Each pair deterministically exchanges every disagreement cluster that raises the better replica's cut, retaining the complement and conserving the pair's summed cut. On the 20,000-spin Gset instance G81, the estimated runtime to reach the certified optimum with 99% success probability (TTS99) was 12.1 s on an 8-core desktop computer. With the same population size, exchange interval and temperature, the method reached the best known cuts on all 17 toroidal Gset graphs, including 9 certified optima. These findings advance ground-state search on large two-dimensional tori by establishing single-temperature RGCX as an efficient population-based method that combines ranked greedy cluster exchange with fixed-temperature Metropolis dynamics.

title: Causality-informed dynamic mode decomposition for unsteady flow analysis
summary: Causal analysis characterizes directional dependencies in dynamical systems, while such information is not typically used to inform reduced-order modeling of unsteady flows. This study proposes a Granger Causality-informed Dynamic Mode Decomposition (GC-DMD) framework that incorporates such information into data-driven modeling and modal analysis of high-dimensional flow data. The framework uses conditional Granger causality estimates to regularize the identification of the DMD operator, preferentially suppressing weakly supported interactions while preserving dynamically relevant couplings. This regularization promotes sparse operators informed by directional predictive dependencies, leading to improved predictive accuracy and identification of dynamically relevant modes. GC-DMD is evaluated on a linear system with a known coupling structure, lid-driven cavity flows with varying dynamical complexity, and a broadband transonic turbulent jet. Compared with standard DMD, GC-DMD improves operator identification accuracy in the linear benchmark and improves the robustness of the identified spectrum while reducing long-horizon prediction errors in the cavity flows. For the turbulent jet, it yields a sparser operator with improved prediction accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of incorporating causality information to guide the identification of sparse, predictive reduced-order models of complex flows. title: Contact-free charge carrier density determination of doped sub-μm thin cubic GaN layers with terahertz time-domain spectroscopy
summary: As cubic GaN is a promising material for optoelectronic applications, its layers need to be precisely doped to realize the desired properties. While contact-based methods are established to measure the realized charge carrier density, contact-free techniques are more advantageous for this purpose. We show terahertz time-domain spectroscopy measurements of cubic GaN layers with thicknesses between 0.6 $μ$m and 2 $μ$m with doping densities in the range from $10^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$ to $10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$. From these measurements, we determine the charge carrier densities and verify the results with time-of-flight secondary-ion mass spectrometry measurements. The results are in accordance with simulations of the doping ranges which the technique is expected to be sensitive in. In preparation for the terahertz time-domain spectroscopy measurements, we validated the layer thicknesses by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy measurements. With this, a wide range of doped cubic GaN samples can be addressed by optical methods. In the future, these techniques could allow for a fast and non-destructive characterization of GaN layers, right after or even during the growth process.

title: Evolutionary tracks and isochrones of the inverse Hall cascade
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables, submitted to J. Plasma Phys
summary: Decaying MHD turbulence can exhibit an inverse cascade, which means that the height of the spectrum of magnetic energy in the subinertial range increases with time. However, there is evidence for a resistive dependence of the inverse transfer speed. It is unclear whether this is caused by reconnection, which is known to depend on resistivity. Here, we show that in the Hall cascade, where no momentum equation is solved, and the induction term is replaced by what corresponds to the negative Lorentz force in MHD, there is still a resistive dependence of the inverse transfer speed, but no such dependence is found for an analogous numerical reconnection experiment. This suggests that the resistive dependence of the inverse transfer speed is not necessarily related to reconnection.

title: Tan's Contact for Trapped Spin-Orbit-Coupled Fermi Gases at Finite Temperature
summary: Tan's contact, bridging microscopic features of many-body quantum systems to two-body contact interactions, is pivotal in the description of quantum gases. However, past studies of Tan's contact of the spin-orbit coupled Fermi gases have been exclusively discussed at zero temperature. The thermal effects on that, which cannot be neglected in most experimental conditions, has not been explored so far. Here, through a path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) study, we show that thermal effects fundamentally alter the scaling relation between spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and Tan's contact. The linear scaling of Tan's contact with respect to the strength of SOC found at zero temperature is drastically undermined by the thermal effects. And a new mechanism based on the competition between the mean occupancy and the energy-reweighted occupancy of the opposite spin fermion pairs within the interaction range has been unveiled, which radically changes the above linear scaling to a non-monotonic dependence. Our work should be useful for future experiments to explore the preternatural thermal effects on Tan's contact of the strongly interacting spin-orbit-coupled Fermi gas.

title: Electric field control of anisotropic spin traffic between spin-filtering and magnon-scattering in a layered antiferromagnet
summary: Layered A-type antiferromagnetic (AFM) semiconductors offer a unique platform for spintronic devices by combining robust magnetism with gate-tunable semiconducting properties. We present a dual-gate field-effect transistor based on CrSBr, a layered A-type AFM with pronounced transport anisotropy and complex spin dynamics. Our device provides independent control over carrier density and displacement field. Systematic transport measurements reveal that the displacement field, rather than doping, predominantly governs the sign and magnitude of magnetoresistance ratio (MRR). We identify the origins of both negative and positive MRR components and connect them to interlayer and intralayer spin-dependent transport mechanisms. We interpret these findings with ab initio calculations and an effective spin-circuit model that reproduces the anisotropic magnetotransport. Our results identify the displacement field as an efficient electrical control parameter of spin transport in CrSBr and suggest that multi-gate architectures could provide similar control in other layered antiferromagnetic semiconductors.

title: Nonlinear dynamics of short-wave instabilities in a helical vortex within and beyond the weakly nonlinear regime
summary: The nonlinear evolution of a helical vortex with axial flow disturbed by an elliptic or curvature instability mode is investigated by direct numerical simulations. The normalized vortex core radius and reduced pitch are systematically varied to examine a wide range of linear growth rates, revealing two types of nonlinear evolution. At relatively small growth rates, both instabilities exhibit weakly nonlinear saturation, with the vortex and unstable mode structures largely preserved. Together with previous findings for other vortex configurations, these results reveal that weakly nonlinear saturation is a generic feature of short-wave instabilities. At larger growth rates, the instabilities reach higher energy levels and evolve beyond the weakly nonlinear regime, with the vortex and unstable mode structures substantially deformed. Comparison with weakly nonlinear analysis suggests that larger linear growth rates require larger disturbance amplitudes for nonlinear effects to balance linear growth. At these larger amplitudes, higher-order nonlinear effects and modal components not retained in the weakly nonlinear analysis become increasingly important, as demonstrated by the numerical results. This provides a new physical interpretation of the departure from the weakly nonlinear regime. Since helical vortices serve as a model for tip vortices shed from rotating blades, these results offer useful insights for tip-vortex control in wind turbines, which can potentially accelerate wake recovery and thereby improve turbine performance.

title: Scale-free wave localization at topological multicriticality
summary: Spatial wave localization at boundaries is conventionally restricted to exponential decay. Here, we observe a scale-free boundary mode exhibiting anomalous polynomial decay, highlighted by strictly linear spatial envelopes, driven by topological multicriticality in acoustic metamaterials. We establish a universal geometric bulk-boundary correspondence rooted in singularity theory by mapping n-th order topological multicriticality onto Arnold An catastrophe. We prove that defectiveness in the spatial transfer matrix enforces a (n-1)-th power spatial decay of boundary modes. At a topological tri-critical point, the singularity of winding function manifests as an A2 fold catastrophe. This dictates a strictly linear spatial decay, marking a sharp departure from the conventional exponential scaling paradigm. Using acoustic metamaterial platforms tuned to a tricritical point, we experimentally demonstrate this linear decay envelope in 1D, and further generalize it to two-dimensional systems to realize scale-free corner modes with simultaneous linear decay along orthogonal directions. While existing critical topology frameworks rely on entanglement spectra to diagnose mode existence in gapless regimes, our work bridges catastrophe theory with topological matter at multicriticalities, advancing the field from abstract mode identification to deterministic real-space wavefunction engineering.

title: Electromagnetic emission at the Langmuir frequency from laser interaction with an unmagnetized plasma
summary: We present the first experimental observation of electromagnetic emission at the Langmuir frequency, $ω_p$, resulting from laser-plasma interaction in an underdense and unmagnetised plasma. The emission is spatially resolved and analyzed in polarization. It originates from an electrostatic wave excited by the Raman instability. Despite its frequency being very close to the plasma's cutoff frequency, $ω_{pe}$, this radiation can escape the plasma by following the decreasing slope of the plasma density profile. Radiation at $2ω_p$, is also observed. This experimental platform offers a powerful tool to explore the processes of wave coupling at the origin of some radio solar bursts.
