title: Adiabatic Variational Principle: Born-Oppenheimer Theory for Emergent Electronic-Order Dynamics
summary: Recent advances in microscopic many-body methods have enabled increasingly accurate descriptions of equilibrium quantum states, yet large-scale simulations of emergent-order dynamics typically rely on phenomenological equations with prescribed free-energy functionals. We introduce the Adiabatic Variational Principle (AVP), a framework for deriving order-parameter dynamics directly from an interacting many-body Hamiltonian. When microscopic relaxation is fast compared with order-parameter evolution, the many-body state follows the collective configuration adiabatically, in analogy with the Born--Oppenheimer separation of electronic and nuclear motion. This assumption makes explicit the adiabatic closure implicit in conventional phase-field descriptions. Each instantaneous order-parameter configuration then defines a constrained quasi-stationary many-body state, and the Lagrange multipliers enforcing these constraints directly provide the thermodynamic forces driving the collective evolution. Nonlinear Mori--Zwanzig projection theory further connects the reversible dynamics to the microscopic algebra of the collective variables and relates dissipation and fluctuations to the eliminated degrees of freedom. Applications to charge- and spin-density-wave dynamics recover Allen--Cahn domain growth, resolve evolving domain networks together with their microscopic electronic structure, and yield generalized Landau--Lifshitz dynamics for itinerant magnetism. The AVP thus provides a solver-independent microscopic foundation for phase-field-like simulations of the nonequilibrium dynamics of emergent electronic order.

title: Transition to turbulence in swirl created by a vertical magnetic field in liquid metal electrodes
summary: Flow transitions in electromagnetically-driven swirl in a cylindrical domain are investigated using three-dimensional simulations for a liquid metal battery electrode. The parameter space considered: applied current $I=11.11-100A$; Current density, $J_0 \approx 4,000-35,000 A/m^2$, domain radius, $R=3-9cm$, domain height, $H=3$ and $4.5cm$). The background magnetic field, $B_0$, strength is varied systematically from 0.1 to 20 G to characterize the route to chaos. \cite{davidson2022swirling} found the onset of chaos occurs around $1-1.5 G$ for aspect ratio $1/6$ and current of 100A, however, this is shifted to $16-17 G$ for a lower current of 16A and aspect ratio $1/2$. Across a range of geometrical configurations and forcing conditions, including variations in aspect ratio, current and current density, a consistent sequence of dynamical transitions is evident from phase portraits, FFT spectrum, 0-1 chaos test, autocorrelation function and correlation dimension. The flow evolution is by the Ruelle--Takens-Newhouse route to chaos, with the strange non-chaotic attractor (SNA) regime providing an intermediate state prior to the onset of chaos. In our results, it is observed that, for a fixed aspect ratio, the transition is governed by a dimensionless group, $Q_m$, representing the ratio of applied Lorentz force to viscous force. The critical value of $Q_m$ at the onset of oscillatory flow is found to be nearly invariant except when the domain height is varied. Moreover, our results follow the $Re \sim Q_m^{2/3}$ scaling law expected from torque balance moderately-forced electro-magnetically driven swirl flows.

AI.tldr: Three-dimensional simulations of electromagnetically driven swirl in a cylindrical liquid-metal battery electrode reveal a consistent Ruelle–Takens–Newhouse route to chaos through a strange non-chaotic attractor, with transitions governed by a Lorentz-to-viscous force ratio Qm and Re ~ Qm^(2/3).
AI.motivation: The paper investigates flow transitions and the route to chaos in electromagnetically driven swirl within a cylindrical domain representing a liquid metal battery electrode, across varied geometry and forcing conditions.
AI.method: The study uses three-dimensional simulations over applied current I=11.11–100 A, current density J0 approximately 4,000–35,000 A/m^2, radius R=3–9 cm, height H=3 and 4.5 cm, and background magnetic field B0 from 0.1 to 20 G. Flow transitions are characterized using phase portraits, FFT spectra, the 0–1 chaos test, autocorrelation functions, and correlation dimension.

The flow evolves via the Ruelle–Takens–Newhouse route to chaos, with a strange non-chaotic attractor regime as an intermediate state. For fixed aspect ratio, the transition is governed by Qm, the ratio of applied Lorentz force to viscous force; the critical Qm at the onset of oscillatory flow is nearly invariant except when domain height is varied. The results moderately follow the Re ~ Qm^(2/3) scaling expected from torque balance. AI.conclusion: The transitions in electromagnetically driven swirl are controlled by the dimensionless group Qm for a fixed aspect ratio, with height variation affecting the critical value, and the observed scaling supports a torque-balance description of moderately forced electromagnetically driven swirl flows.

title: Multistable nematic liquid crystal pores as reconfigurable optical vortex metasurfaces
summary: Nematic liquid crystals confined in cylindrical pores adopt multiple stable director topologies --- radial, escaped, and arches --- each imprinting a distinct optical signature on transmitted circularly polarized light, with topological charge set by the projected director winding number, $\ell = 2m$. Landau--de Gennes simulations further demonstrate that an applied electric field switches the pore between topologies, and hence between their near-field optical signatures. Because each topology is locally stable, sub-wavelength NLC pore arrays constitute an electrically reconfigurable, non-volatile platform for topology-encoded near-field optical readout, with potential application to optical labeling and anti-counterfeiting.

title: Magnetic shocks generated by two counterstreaming plasma jets induced by an intense femtosecond laser pulse
summary: This work extends the investigation of magnetic control of counterstreaming laser-produced plasma jets reported in Zemskov et al. (2026), focusing on the experiments performed in the presence of a uniform 14 T magnetic field oriented transverse to the jet propagation. When generating plasma flows using 60-80 fs, 10-15 J pulses at the PEARL facility, we observe the formation of narrow, stationary layers with strong magnetic-field amplification and sharp plasma-density gradients in the interaction region. We interpret these features as the result of compressing the externally applied transverse field by the converging plasma ram pressure. The external magnetic field is advected and compressed until its magnetic pressure balances the decreasing ram pressure of the jets. Time-resolved interferometry, shadowgraphy, and Faraday polarimetry, combined with hybrid PIC--fluid simulations, reproduce the formation of a high-field barrier that decelerates and laterally redirects plasma flows while producing multiple density jumps. We discuss the astrophysical implications: the compression of an initially weak ambient field by converging flows provides an efficient, non-turbulent channel for magnetic-field amplification that can render interstellar magnetic fields dynamically important - a condition essential for diffusive shock acceleration in supernova remnants. Our experiments therefore establish a laboratory platform bridging externally magnetized and self-magnetized regimes and offer a complementary route to magnetic-field amplification in high-energy astrophysical shocks.

title: Static Response of the Strongly Coupled Electron Gas from Diffusion Monte Carlo
summary: The local field factor $G(q)$ of the HEG describes how exchange and correlation modify the response to a static perturbation, and enters dielectric screening, effective electron--electron interactions, and the xc kernel of TDDFT. Accurate zero-temperature data for $G(q)$, however, remain limited to metallic densities, $r_s\leq10$. In this work, we present diffusion Monte Carlo calculations of the static density response function $χ(q)$ and of $G(q)$ for $2\leq r_s\leq100$, and describe and discuss the methodological steps that enabled these calculations. We show how optimization of the perturbing potential in the trial wave function has an important effect, as a poor choice can reverse the sign of the response. A closed-form expression is provided for its optimal value, together with the density dependence of the linear-response window. We further show that backflow correlations leave $χ(q)$ unchanged and that $G(q)$ depends only weakly on system size even at very low density, so that Slater--Jastrow wave functions and modest system sizes suffice. Together, these results provide a practical guide for future QMC calculations of response properties of the electron gas and real materials. Our results agree with previous DMC data at metallic densities for $q>k_F$, and extend them below $k_F$. They also agree with diagrammatic QMC at $r_s=2$. At lower densities, our results show that $G(q)$ develops a nonmonotonic structure at intermediate-$q$, where the response approaches that of the noninteracting gas. Quantitative agreement is seen with finite-temperature path integral Monte Carlo, suggesting that the previously reported finite-temperature structure is inherited from the ground state. Using a parametrization of $G(q)$ that reproduces our data throughout the liquid phase, we relate this structure to short-range order in the pair correlation function and the static structure factor.

title: Numerical analysis of geometrical effect on drop deformation and breakup between rotating cylinders
summary: This study numerically investigates the effects of geometrical curvature on drop deformation and breakup in shear flow between counter-rotating concentric cylinders. Simulations were performed using a geometric Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) method incorporating plicRDF interface reconstruction and isoAdvector interface advection, combined with adaptive mesh refinement. Three circular geometries with different values of the non-dimensional geometrical curvature, $κ_{\mathrm F}$, were considered and compared with a planar shear flow system. At fixed Reynolds and Capillary numbers ($Re$ and $Ca$), the breakup morphology differed substantially between the planar and circular systems. In the planar system, the drop underwent relatively symmetric neck thinning, whereas in the circular systems, the drop exhibited asymmetric deformation and pronounced azimuthal elongation. At higher curvature, the drop formed a thin filament that subsequently fragmented, producing multiple satellite drops. Analysis of the internal velocity field and the magnitude of the rate-of-deformation tensor revealed distinct flow and deformation structures associated with these breakup behaviors. Furthermore, the critical $Re$ for breakup, $Re_{\mathrm{cr}}$, decreased with increasing $κ_{\mathrm F}$ at nvestigated $Ca$ values. In contrast, the maximum dimensionless elongation length immediately before breakup at $Re=Re_{\mathrm{cr}}$ increased with $κ_{\mathrm F}$. These findings suggest that geometrical curvature affects not only the breakup threshold but also the deformation process leading to breakup, providing insights into drop breakup in curved shear flows.

Geometrical curvature produces asymmetric, azimuthally elongated deformation, filament fragmentation and satellite drops at higher curvature; the critical Re for breakup decreases with curvature, while the maximum dimensionless elongation immediately before breakup at Re_cr increases with curvature.

title: Unlimited-Range Absolute Distance Interferometry Outdoors via Tunable Synthetic and Pseudo-Supersynthetic Wavelengths: The TeleYAG-II Interferometer
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, research data openly available under the following DOI: https://doi.org/10.7795/720.20261014
summary: Absolute distance interferometry requires an unlimited non-ambiguity range to be truly absolute. Tunable synthetic wavelength interferometry allows for the construction of pseudo-supersynthetic wavelengths using a limited number of optical sources and a standard interferometer setup. This approach facilitates the creation of a series of consecutively deployable synthetic wavelengths, ultimately combining macroscopic unambiguity with microscopic interferometric accuracy. We have implemented and demonstrated this concept in the TeleYAG-II interferometer, designed as an SI-traceable standard for the calibration of geodetic baselines. The system employs two Nd:YAG lasers as optical sources, with their frequency difference controlled by a versatile optical phase-locked loop. Specifically engineered for robustness in field conditions, the heterodyne interferometer was validated through an outdoor measurement campaign. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the method, achieving an expanded measurement uncertainty of 0.13 mm over a distance of 224 m without the need for auxiliary length measurements.

title: Linear-Stability-Guided Two-Stage Surrogate Model for Nonlinear ITG-TEM Turbulence
summary: We develop a two-stage surrogate model framework to predict the linear and nonlinear properties of ITG-TEM turbulence from GENE gyrokinetic simulations. The first stage uses a hierarchical ensemble of stability and mode classifiers, along with global and mode-specific regressors, to predict the linear growth rate and real frequency. The second stage uses these predictions as linear spectra in a Fourier neural operator (FNO)-based nonlinear surrogate model. The nonlinear model predicts saturated potential and heat flux spectra, together with zonal flow quantities. Two linear drive scalars, the maximum and integral of the linear growth rate over a low-wavenumber range, are also supplied directly to the networks predicting scalar quantities. For the architecture studied here, comparisons with models omitting either or both input paths show that linear information can improve spectral and scalar predictions under extrapolation toward stronger linear drive.

title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo
comment: Main document 9 pages, 6 figures, supplementary information 14 pages, 13 figures, to appear on PRB
summary: We use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods to investigate the lowest neutral excitation of solid molecular hydrogen in phase-I under increasing compression, with emphasis on structural and response properties. We employ QMC wave functions for the excited state that feature only a single orbital substitution, or a multideterminant expansion including every single particle-hole transition, and compare the results with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) and time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). We examine a number of nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations. The effect of the multideterminant expansion is marginal on the QMC excitation energies but crucial on the exciton localization and related quantities, irrespective of full optimization and imaginary time projection. In the strong insulating regime at low density, multideterminant QMC results match and in some cases surpass the degree of localization afforded by BSE. A similar trend is observed for transition dipole moments and excitation-induced forces, with generally good agreement between QMC and BSE but marked discrepancies for nuclear configurations where localization differs significantly. TDDFT generally gives a more extended exciton with correspondingly weaker transition dipole moments. These differences decrease upon compression, as the system approaches a semiconducting regime where multiple particle-hole transitions are less important.

title: Triadic energy cascades and linear amplification mechanisms in supersonic turbulent boundary layers over curved walls
summary: Direct numerical simulations are performed to investigate supersonic turbulent boundary layers subjected to continuous concave and convex surface curvatures. Scale-resolved spectral turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) budgets, triadic energy-transfer bispectra, spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD), and global resolvent analysis are employed to elucidate the effects of compressibility and pressure gradients, and to distinguish the linear and nonlinear mechanisms at play. Over concave walls, the destabilizing curvature enhances pressure-strain redistribution, shifting near-wall turbulence toward a two-component state, and induces a shear-driven outer-layer production peak at low spanwise wavenumbers. Bispectral and SPOD analyses reveal that this outer-layer energy feeds a structured, multi-step triadic transfer toward fundamental large-scale and spanwise-uniform modes, which physically manifests as streamwise vortex breakdown rather than a three-dimensional inverse cascade. Global resolvent analysis further demonstrates that while nonlinear triadic interactions select the dominant scale amplitudes, the spatial topology of these coherent structures is dictated by linear mean-flow receptivity and spatially developing convective instabilities. Conversely, over convex walls, stabilizing curvature and dilatation attenuate pressure fluctuations and suppress pressure-strain redistribution, breaking the near-wall turbulent cycle and trapping energy within elongated, one-component streamwise streaks, while a localized resolvent wavemaker energizes the downstream recovery region.

AI.motivation: The study aims to elucidate how continuous concave and convex surface curvature, compressibility, and pressure gradients affect supersonic turbulent boundary layers, and to distinguish linear from nonlinear mechanisms governing coherent structure dynamics and energy transfer.

title: Ghosts in the nanomachine: dynamical slowing-down in the phase-space of nanomechanical strings
summary: The linear behavior of micro- and nanomechanical devices has been the topic of intense study over the past years. Their nonlinear behavior, on the other hand, continues to provide new and interesting dynamics. This work leverages a cavity opto-mechanical system whose very high sensitivity and low dissipation rate allows to capture the dynamics of fast transients that occur when strongly-driven nonlinear resonators relax to their equilibrium state. We experimentally study the ringdown dynamics of a nanomechanical Duffing resonator in both the time domain and in phase space. The resonator exhibits very different ringdown dynamics depending on whether it is subject to one or two tone driving. In the former case the ringdown follows a regular exponential decay, whereas the latter case shows exotic dynamics such as libration, slowing-down while scattering in phase-space, and ghost slowing-down. We demonstrate that this distinct difference can be attributed to the structure of the phase space itself. Surprisingly, we find that the energy in the resonator changes non-monotonously and that long delay between turning off the drive and the decay of the motion amplitude results in dynamical meta-states.

One-tone driving produces regular exponential decay, while two-tone driving produces exotic dynamics such as libration, phase-space scattering with slowing-down, and ghost slowing-down; these differences are attributed to phase-space structure. The work also reports non-monotonic energy evolution and dynamical meta-states.

The paper aims to capture fast transient dynamics that occur when strongly driven nonlinear resonators relax to equilibrium, using a system with very high sensitivity and low dissipation.

title: High-Repetition-Rate Laser-Driven Fast Neutron Generation from Planar Liquid Heavy Water Jets
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures. F. Treffert and G. D. Glenn contributed equally to this work
summary: We demonstrate a high-repetition-rate, directional pitcher-catcher neutron source employing a continuously flowing, ambient-temperature liquid jet pitcher and a beryllium catcher target. Proton or deuteron beams are accelerated at 0.5 Hz from water (H$_{2}$O) or heavy water (D$_{2}$O) sheet jets using the $2ω$ ALEPH laser at Colorado State University. Deuteron-induced neutron generation shows an average flux enhancement in the target normal direction of 13x compared to proton-induced neutron generation, achieving peak fluxes of $7.9\times10^{5}$ neutrons/sr. The experimentally predicted ion-to-neutron conversion efficiency of 1.5$\times 10^{-5}$ for protons and 1.1$\times 10^{-3}$ for deuterons indicates a significant yield contribution from the deuteron breakup reaction. High shot-to-shot stability neutron spectra up to 8.7~MeV ($^9$Be(d,n)$^{10}$B) are observed for more than 200 consecutive shots.

title: RAKI: High-Order Alternative Finite Differences for General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics
summary: Binary neutron star (BNS) and black hole--neutron star mergers are among the most important multimessenger sources. Observations of these events could provide valuable insights into several unresolved phenomena, ranging from the efficiency of magnetic field amplification during and after mergers to the formation of magnetars and jets. Understanding these phenomena requires accurate modelling of magnetic field evolution, which remains a challenge for state-of-the-art general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations. In this work, we present \texttt{RAKI} (Relativistic Astrophysics Code Implementation of the Alternative Finite Difference Approach for GRMHD), the first GRMHD code to simulate BNS mergers using high-order alternative finite-difference methods with adaptive-order WENO (AFD-WENO-AO) reconstruction and a fully non-staggered, node-centred vector-potential formulation. The code achieves up to ninth-order convergence in smooth test problems while accurately capturing discontinuities. In magnetised Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff (TOV) star tests, \texttt{RAKI} retains $99.2$ per cent of the initial maximum magnetic field strength over ${\sim}2$ ms, exhibiting an order of magnitude less magnetic field loss than a reference GRMHD code at the same resolution. In BNS merger simulations, fifth-order AFD-WENO-AO reconstruction yields approximately third-order convergence of the gravitational-wave phase in both magnetised and unmagnetised models. The discrete no-monopole constraint is preserved to machine precision without staggered grids, even during BNS mergers with moving refinement regions. These results establish \texttt{RAKI} as a high-order, non-staggered GRMHD framework for accurate modelling of magnetic field evolution in neutron star mergers and its implications for multimessenger astrophysics.

They evaluate it on smooth and discontinuous test problems, magnetised Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff star tests, and magnetised and unmagnetised binary neutron star merger simulations.

title: From Dye to Dynamics: Quantitative Measurements of Fluid Flows from Vortex Geometry
comment: This work supported by NSF grant 2330349
summary: Although vorticity and passive tracers (such as dye) are both transported by fluid flows, there are subtle differences in how this transport happens. This indicates that dye cannot be used to track vortex motion in experiments, even though it has often been used for this purpose. In this manuscript we show that under proper circumstances dye can be used to accurately track the center-lines of vortex filaments. Moreover, we show that a number of important fluid quantities, such as energy and helicity, can be computed in terms of the shape of the vortex center-line. As a result, dye-tracked vortices are a valuable tool for measuring the properties of fluid motion in a variety of experimental situations. Moreover, we discuss techniques by which could be used to extract more detailed vortex information in future work.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that, under appropriate conditions, dye can accurately track vortex filament center-lines, enabling energy and helicity to be computed from center-line shape and making dye-tracked vortices useful for experimental fluid measurements.
AI.motivation: Vorticity and passive tracers such as dye are both transported by fluid flows, but their transport differs subtly; dye is often used to track vortex motion even though it cannot generally do so, motivating an assessment of when dye can reliably track vortex filaments.
AI.method: The authors show that under proper circumstances dye can accurately track the center-lines of vortex filaments, express important fluid quantities including energy and helicity in terms of the vortex center-line shape, and discuss techniques for extracting more detailed vortex information in future work. Specific experimental conditions and techniques are not provided in the abstract.
AI.result: Dye can accurately track vortex center-lines under suitable circumstances; energy and helicity can be computed from the shape of the vortex center-line; and dye-tracked vortices are therefore valuable for measuring properties of fluid motion in a variety of experimental situations.
AI.conclusion: Dye-tracked vortices provide a useful experimental tool for measuring fluid-motion properties, and future work may use discussed techniques to extract more detailed vortex information.

title: Scattering-force-driven light-sheet fluorescence microscopy for scan-free three-dimensional imaging
summary: Optical manipulation offers a powerful non-contact approach to precise positioning, directional transport and three-dimensional (3D) imaging of microscale objects. However, positional fluctuations during optical confinement introduce spatial sampling errors that compromise imaging quality and acquisition speed. Here, we demonstrate a scattering-force-driven optical manipulation imaging method that replaces the stepwise scanning of conventional optical trapping with continuous directional transport of microparticles. An axial scattering force generated by a low-numerical-aperture focused beam propels microparticles through a light sheet, while their positions and fluorescence signals are simultaneously recorded to establish direct spatial correspondence between particle motion and tomographic images. Experiments demonstrate that this approach reduces the effects of positional fluctuations on 3D imaging, achieving an axial sampling interval of 0.1 μm and an imaging rate of 250 Hz. The method also enables effective imaging of samples with diverse structural features while reducing optical power requirements by 70%. By combining robust spatial sampling, high-speed acquisition and reduced photodamage, this approach offers a promising route to rapid 3D imaging, dynamic observation and microscale spatial analysis of microparticles and biological specimens.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a scattering-force-driven optical manipulation imaging method that continuously transports microparticles through a light sheet instead of using stepwise optical trapping, enabling faster and more robust 3D imaging with reduced positional-fluctuation artifacts.
AI.motivation: Optical manipulation enables non-contact positioning, directional transport, and 3D imaging of microscale objects, but positional fluctuations during optical confinement introduce spatial sampling errors that compromise imaging quality and acquisition speed.
AI.method: A low-numerical-aperture focused beam generates an axial scattering force that propels microparticles continuously through a light sheet. Particle positions and fluorescence signals are recorded simultaneously, establishing direct spatial correspondence between particle motion and tomographic images and replacing conventional stepwise scanning in optical trapping.
AI.result: The approach reduces the effects of positional fluctuations on 3D imaging, achieves an axial sampling interval of 0.1 μm and an imaging rate of 250 Hz, enables effective imaging of samples with diverse structural features, and reduces optical power requirements by 70%.
AI.conclusion: By combining robust spatial sampling, high-speed acquisition, and reduced photodamage, the method offers a promising route to rapid 3D imaging, dynamic observation, and microscale spatial analysis of microparticles and biological specimens.

title: Local neoclassical calculations using a Hermite-Laguerre velocity-space basis with advanced collision operators
summary: We present radially local neoclassical (NC) calculations based on a Hermite-Laguerre (HL) velocity-space polynomial expansion combined with advanced linearized collision operators, including the exact Fokker-Planck-Landau (FPL) operator. The implementation is verified against the NC code SFINCS using both a multi-species Lenard-Bernstein-Dougherty-like (LBD) operator and the FPL operator, the NC fluxes agreeing to within 3% in the Pfirsch-Schlüter regime. The accuracy of the HL basis is then assessed by convergence studies against the Legendre-Laguerre (LG) basis. At an equal number of spectral coefficients, neither basis is uniformly more accurate. In the plateau regime, the LG basis is more accurate on the particle and heat fluxes, which are sensitive to the trapped-passing boundary, whereas the HL basis is more accurate on the bootstrap current, carried by the parallel flow. In the banana regime, both bases converge slowly. Finally, we compare the LBD and the original (OS) and improved Sugama (IS) operators against the FPL operator. The IS operator retrieves the NC fluxes to within 6% over four decades of collisionality, whereas the LBD operator overestimates the ion heat flux by a factor of 2.6 to 4.7. The OS operator overestimates the ion heat flux by 4 to 33%, while retrieving the particle flux and the bootstrap current to within 9% and 18%, respectively. The convention adopted for the LBD collision frequency also changes the bootstrap current by up to two orders of magnitude. The present work extends the use of the HL basis, previously used in turbulent calculations, to NC physics and, to the knowledge of the author, these are the first NC calculations using the HL basis.

AI.tldr: The paper implements radially local neoclassical calculations using a Hermite-Laguerre velocity-space expansion with advanced linearized collision operators, including the exact Fokker-Planck-Landau operator. It verifies the implementation against SFINCS, compares the Hermite-Laguerre and Legendre-Laguerre bases, and benchmarks approximate collision operators against the exact Fokker-Planck-Landau operator.
AI.motivation: The work aims to extend the Hermite-Laguerre basis, previously used in turbulent calculations, to neoclassical physics and to assess its accuracy and that of approximate collision operators against the exact Fokker-Planck-Landau operator. According to the abstract, these are the first neoclassical calculations using the Hermite-Laguerre basis.
AI.method: Radially local neoclassical calculations are performed using a Hermite-Laguerre velocity-space polynomial expansion combined with advanced linearized collision operators, including the exact Fokker-Planck-Landau operator. The implementation is verified against the SFINCS code using a multi-species Lenard-Bernstein-Dougherty-like operator and the Fokker-Planck-Landau operator. Convergence studies compare the Hermite-Laguerre basis with the Legendre-Laguerre basis, and the Lenard-Bernstein-Dougherty-like, original Sugama, and improved Sugama operators are compared with the Fokker-Planck-Landau operator.
AI.result: Neoclassical fluxes agree with SFINCS to within 3% in the Pfirsch-Schlüter regime. At equal numbers of spectral coefficients, neither basis is uniformly more accurate: in the plateau regime the Legendre-Laguerre basis is more accurate for particle and heat fluxes sensitive to the trapped-passing boundary, while the Hermite-Laguerre basis is more accurate for the bootstrap current carried by parallel flow; in the banana regime both bases converge slowly. The improved Sugama operator retrieves neoclassical fluxes to within 6% over four decades of collisionality. The Lenard-Bernstein-Dougherty-like operator overestimates the ion heat flux by a factor of 2.6 to 4.7. The original Sugama operator overestimates the ion heat flux by 4 to 33%, while retrieving the particle flux and bootstrap current to within 9% and 18%, respectively. The convention adopted for the Lenard-Bernstein-Dougherty-like collision frequency changes the bootstrap current by up to two orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The Hermite-Laguerre basis is successfully extended from turbulent calculations to neoclassical physics, with the abstract stating that these are the first neoclassical calculations using this basis. The choice of velocity-space basis and collision operator materially affects neoclassical fluxes and currents; the improved Sugama operator performs best among the approximate operators examined, whereas the Lenard-Bernstein-Dougherty-like operator and collision-frequency convention can produce large errors.

title: Optimization of curved vortex generator geometry for enhanced thermal performance in water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger
summary: In the study, the geometry of curved rectangular vortex generators (RVG) has been optimized to enhance heat transfer and overall performance of the analyzed water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger (FTHE). The developed and validated conjugate numerical model includes a small section of the full-scale heat exchanger representing the computational domain, with fully developed velocity and temperature profiles specified at the inlet boundaries of the water. Four influential geometry parameters of the vortex generator were selected for the optimization; attack angle, curvature angle, axial position in the streamwise direction and height. The optimization process has been performed according to two criteria: maximization of heat transfer solely and maximization of heat transfer while considering the influence of pressure drop. Accordingly, one objective function related to the Colburn factor (j) and two objective functions combining the Colburn factor and the friction factor (f) were defined. The regression analysis has been used and the Central composite design of experiment was selected in order to obtain non-linear regression polynomial functions which were integrated into the investigated objectives. The optimization procedure has been performed using the genetic algorithm. Optimized configurations performance improvement was evaluated through comparison with the performance of the reference FTHE with plain fins. For the RVG configuration optimized according to the objective of maximizing heat transfer, the Colburn factor was enhanced by 53.1%. Optimizing the RVG configuration to maximize heat transfer while accounting for the influence of pressure drop resulted in an enhancement of the FTHE area goodness factor by 14.4% for one set of geometry parameters, and an enhancement of volume goodness factor by 26.5% for another.

AI.tldr: Curved rectangular vortex generators were geometry-optimized for a water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger using a validated conjugate model, central composite design regression, and a genetic algorithm; optimization maximized either heat transfer alone or heat transfer with pressure-drop effects. Heat transfer rose by 53.1% in the heat-transfer-only case, while pressure-drop-aware optimization improved area goodness factor by 14.4% and volume goodness factor by 26.5% for different geometry sets.
AI.motivation: The study aims to enhance heat transfer and overall performance of the analyzed water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger by optimizing the geometry of curved rectangular vortex generators, including consideration of pressure-drop influence.
AI.method: A developed and validated conjugate numerical model was used, representing a small section of the full-scale heat exchanger with fully developed velocity and temperature profiles specified at the water inlet boundaries. Four vortex-generator geometry parameters were optimized: attack angle, curvature angle, axial streamwise position, and height. Objective functions used the Colburn factor j and combinations of j and the friction factor f. Regression analysis with a central composite design of experiments produced nonlinear regression polynomials integrated into the objectives, and a genetic algorithm performed the optimization. Optimized configurations were compared with a reference plain-fin heat exchanger.
AI.result: For the RVG configuration optimized solely to maximize heat transfer, the Colburn factor increased by 53.1%. When pressure-drop influence was included, optimization improved the finned-tube heat exchanger area goodness factor by 14.4% for one set of geometry parameters and the volume goodness factor by 26.5% for another.
AI.conclusion: Optimized curved rectangular vortex generator geometries can substantially enhance heat transfer and, when pressure drop is considered, improve overall goodness factors relative to a plain-fin reference configuration; the two pressure-drop-aware outcomes correspond to different geometry parameter sets.

title: Inherent Failure Modes of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Buoyancy-Driven Flow: Role of Non-Dimensionalization in Network Training
summary: We investigate the influence of non-dimensionalization on the trainability and accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for buoyancy-driven flows. Using a differentially heated square cavity at $\mathrm{Pr}=0.71$ and $\mathrm{Ra}=10^3$--$10^5$, we compare thermal-diffusive and free-fall velocity scalings under identical training conditions. The free-fall scaling, with a unit buoyancy coefficient, achieves errors below 1.1\% in the mean Nusselt number for $\mathrm{Ra}\le10^4$, whereas the diffusive scaling, with a buoyancy coefficient of $\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr}$, produces errors of 157--650\% and diverges at $\mathrm{Ra}=10^5$. We identify a coefficient-induced gradient imbalance, with the dominant buoyancy-related contribution to the loss gradient scaling as $(\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr})^2$, and confirm it through direct gradient measurements. Neither sparse-data supervision nor adaptive loss weighting resolves the training difficulties under the tested conditions. For unsteady convection, the free-fall PINN accurately predicts long-time heat transfer but fails to capture the transient Nusselt-number overshoot. These findings establish non-dimensionalization as an important design consideration for improving PINN trainability in buoyancy-driven flows.

AI.tldr: The paper compares thermal-diffusive and free-fall non-dimensionalizations for PINNs on buoyancy-driven cavity flow. Free-fall scaling is far more trainable and accurate, while diffusive scaling causes a gradient imbalance, large errors, and divergence at high Ra; transient Nusselt overshoot remains unresolved.
AI.motivation: The study investigates how non-dimensionalization affects the trainability and accuracy of physics-informed neural networks for buoyancy-driven flows, aiming to identify it as a design consideration for improving PINN performance.
AI.method: Using a differentially heated square cavity at Pr=0.71 and Ra=10^3 to 10^5, the authors compare thermal-diffusive and free-fall velocity scalings under identical training conditions. They measure loss gradients directly, test sparse-data supervision and adaptive loss weighting, and evaluate unsteady convection.
AI.result: Free-fall scaling with a unit buoyancy coefficient gives mean Nusselt-number errors below 1.1% for Ra<=10^4, whereas diffusive scaling with buoyancy coefficient Ra Pr gives errors of 157-650% and diverges at Ra=10^5. The dominant buoyancy-related loss-gradient contribution scales as (Ra Pr)^2. Neither sparse-data supervision nor adaptive loss weighting resolves the training difficulties. For unsteady convection, the free-fall PINN predicts long-time heat transfer accurately but misses the transient Nusselt-number overshoot.
AI.conclusion: Non-dimensionalization is an important design consideration for improving PINN trainability in buoyancy-driven flows.

title: Edge intelligence for distributed acoustic sensing with ultracompact neural networks
summary: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) transforms optical fibres into dense arrays of vibration sensors for continuous, long-range monitoring with high spatial resolution. Yet converting these large-scale measurements into actionable information with compact models that retain task performance remains challenging. Existing artificial-intelligence approaches are typically optimized for specific sensing environments and tasks, but their computational requirements can hinder deployment in compact, power-constrained field systems. Here, we introduce DAS-NanoNet, a framework that automatically constructs lightweight neural networks for different DAS scenarios and tasks, together with OmniDAS, an open benchmark spanning six representative environments. Using lightweight temporal operators tailored to DAS signals, an adaptive neural architecture search strategy derives a compact network for each scenario-task pairing. Across classification, localization, compression, and denoising tasks in diverse DAS applications, DAS-NanoNet consistently yields highly compact architectures. On a six-class dataset, it achieves 99.68% accuracy with only 1,391 trainable parameters, while delivering comparable or better performance with up to 18,098-fold fewer parameters than previously reported high-accuracy networks. Its compact architecture further enables edge deployment, achieving sub 9 $μ$s inference latency on the deployed hardware platform across different DAS applications. DAS-NanoNet provides a route towards edge intelligence for compact, low-power and real-time DAS systems through ultracompact networks tailored to individual sensing scenarios and tasks.

AI.tldr: DAS-NanoNet automatically constructs ultracompact neural networks tailored to different distributed acoustic sensing scenarios and tasks, supported by the OmniDAS six-environment benchmark. It achieves highly compact models across classification, localization, compression, and denoising, including 99.68% accuracy on a six-class dataset with only 1,391 trainable parameters and sub-9 μs edge inference latency.
AI.motivation: DAS turns optical fibres into dense vibration-sensor arrays for continuous, long-range, high-resolution monitoring, but converting large-scale measurements into actionable information with compact models that retain task performance is challenging. Existing AI approaches are typically optimized for specific sensing environments and tasks, and their computational requirements can hinder deployment in compact, power-constrained field systems.
AI.method: The paper introduces DAS-NanoNet, a framework that automatically constructs lightweight neural networks for different DAS scenarios and tasks, together with OmniDAS, an open benchmark spanning six representative environments. It uses lightweight temporal operators tailored to DAS signals and an adaptive neural architecture search strategy to derive a compact network for each scenario-task pairing.
AI.result: Across classification, localization, compression, and denoising tasks in diverse DAS applications, DAS-NanoNet consistently yields highly compact architectures. On a six-class dataset, it achieves 99.68% accuracy with only 1,391 trainable parameters, while delivering comparable or better performance with up to 18,098-fold fewer parameters than previously reported high-accuracy networks. Its compact architecture also enables edge deployment, achieving sub-9 μs inference latency on the deployed hardware platform across different DAS applications.
AI.conclusion: DAS-NanoNet provides a route toward edge intelligence for compact, low-power, and real-time DAS systems through ultracompact networks tailored to individual sensing scenarios and tasks.

title: Options for heating, fueling, and current drive in MANTA, a high-field negative triangularity fusion pilot plant
comment: 22 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to Plasma Physics and Controlled Fusion. To be presented at APS-DPP 2026 Annual Meeting
summary: In this work, we assess how the performance of MANTA, a high-field, highly radiative, negative triangularity tokamak concept, depends on pellet fueling, ion cyclotron resonant frequency (ICRF) heating, and lower hybrid current drive (LHCD) schemes. Negative triangularity (NT) has been gaining momentum in the fusion community as a naturally, robustly ELM-free regime that is capable of power plant level performance. The MANTA device has been the subject of previous works regarding the whole-device design, power handling and divertor assessments, and core transport optimizations. Informed by these previous studies, we assess whether changes to the original MANTA heating and current drive scheme can positively affect performance, both in terms of lowering scrape-off layer power (improving power-handling, a primary benefit of NT) and maximizing plasma gain to levels necessary for an attractive fusion pilot plant. In this work, we find that the MANTA concept can yield improved performance in terms of plasma gain and scrape-off layer power by simultaneously going to lower input power and higher seeded impurity fraction. Also, we find that increasing the fueling magnitude can increase fusion power while minimally impacting scrape-off layer power. Performance can also be improved by optimizing the ICRF design; decreasing the minority ion fraction, decreasing the toroidal mode number of the injected wave, and switching from a helium-3 minority ion to a hydrogen-1 minority ion all result in increases to fusion power. The additional inboard space afforded by the NT geometry provides an opportunity for wave launch to be moved to the inboard side. This is beneficial for LHCD access and results in a wide range of potential current profiles in the edge, with the total driven current due to 25 MW of LHCD reaching up to 1.2 MA, or about 12% of the total current.

AI.tldr: The paper assesses how pellet fueling, ICRF heating, and LHCD schemes affect the performance of MANTA, a high-field, highly radiative negative-triangularity tokamak concept. It finds that lower input power with higher seeded impurity fraction improves plasma gain and scrape-off-layer power, stronger fueling raises fusion power with little SOL penalty, ICRF optimization increases fusion power, and inboard LHCD launch enabled by negative triangularity improves current-drive access and can drive up to 1.2 MA with 25 MW.
AI.motivation: Negative triangularity is attractive as a naturally ELM-free regime capable of power-plant-level performance. MANTA has been studied previously for whole-device design, power handling, divertor assessment, and core transport optimization. This work asks whether changes to the original MANTA heating and current-drive scheme can improve performance by lowering scrape-off-layer power and maximizing plasma gain for an attractive fusion pilot plant.
AI.method: The abstract states that the authors assess the dependence of MANTA performance on pellet fueling, ICRF heating, and LHCD schemes, informed by prior MANTA whole-device, power-handling, divertor, and core-transport studies. They evaluate changes to the original heating and current-drive design in terms of plasma gain and scrape-off-layer power. The abstract does not provide specific simulation codes, models, or quantitative parameter-scan details.
AI.result: Improved plasma gain and scrape-off-layer power were found by simultaneously using lower input power and a higher seeded impurity fraction. Increasing the fueling magnitude increased fusion power while only minimally affecting scrape-off-layer power. ICRF performance improved—increasing fusion power—by decreasing the minority ion fraction, decreasing the toroidal mode number of the injected wave, and switching from a helium-3 minority ion to a hydrogen-1 minority ion. Negative-triangularity geometry provides additional inboard space for wave launch, benefiting LHCD access and enabling a wide range of edge current profiles; 25 MW of LHCD drives up to 1.2 MA, about 12% of the total current.
AI.conclusion: The MANTA concept can achieve improved performance in plasma gain and scrape-off-layer power through coordinated changes to fueling, seeding, ICRF design, and LHCD launch. The results indicate that lower input power with higher impurity seeding, increased fueling, optimized ICRF minority species and wave parameters, and inboard LHCD launch are beneficial for MANTA performance.

title: Transformer-inspired architectures make machine-learned electron densities accurate and transferable enough to bypass self-consistency
comment: 36 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables; Extended Data (4 figures, 2 tables) and Supplementary Information included
summary: We introduce machine learning models that accurately predict the electron density, the central variable of density functional theory. They are built on Transformer-inspired architectures, which require little computation per parameter and can therefore be enlarged at low cost. The proposed models, SwinUNETR-V2 and its attention-free counterpart NeXtUNETR, achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on QM9, with normalized mean absolute errors in the density averaging 0.075% and 0.046%, respectively. The predicted densities are accurate enough to bypass the self-consistent iteration: a single Kohn-Sham step reproduces the self-consistent electronic structure. For NeXtUNETR, the median errors are 0.036 meV in the total energy, 0.65 meV/angstrom in the forces and 1.8 meV in the HOMO-LUMO gap. The forces not only recover the self-consistent minima in geometry optimization but also successfully drive ab initio molecular dynamics. Fine-tuned on small datasets, both networks also transfer accurately to systems containing elements absent from QM9 or larger than its molecules.

AI.tldr: Transformer-inspired SwinUNETR-V2 and NeXtUNETR predict DFT electron densities with state-of-the-art QM9 accuracy, enabling a single Kohn-Sham step to reproduce self-consistent electronic structure and supporting geometry optimization, molecular dynamics, and transfer learning.
AI.motivation: The paper targets accurate machine-learning prediction of the electron density, which is the central variable of density functional theory. The abstract does not provide further explicit motivation.
AI.method: The authors introduce Transformer-inspired architectures, SwinUNETR-V2 and the attention-free NeXtUNETR, designed to require little computation per parameter and to be enlarged at low cost. The models are evaluated on QM9 and fine-tuned on small datasets for transfer to other systems.
AI.result: SwinUNETR-V2 and NeXtUNETR achieve state-of-the-art QM9 density accuracy with normalized mean absolute errors averaging 0.075% and 0.046%, respectively. A single Kohn-Sham step reproduces the self-consistent electronic structure. For NeXtUNETR, median errors are 0.036 meV in total energy, 0.65 meV/angstrom in forces, and 1.8 meV in the HOMO-LUMO gap. The forces recover self-consistent geometry-optimization minima and drive ab initio molecular dynamics. After fine-tuning on small datasets, both networks transfer accurately to systems with elements absent from QM9 or larger than its molecules.
AI.conclusion: Machine-learning models can predict DFT electron densities accurately enough to bypass self-consistent iteration, yielding accurate energies, forces, and gaps and supporting geometry optimization, ab initio molecular dynamics, and transfer learning beyond QM9.

title: Regional accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for recirculation in a deep lid-driven cavity
summary: Deep lid-driven cavities contain strong motion beneath the lid and much weaker recirculation at depth, so agreement in bulk velocity is an incomplete assessment of a computed flow. We examine data-free physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for steady, two-dimensional incompressible flow in a cavity of depth-to-width ratio five at Reynolds numbers 100, 250, 500 and 1000. An established hard-constrained streamfunction formulation is combined with prescribed regional collocation, transferred initialization, and selected residual-scaling and envelope variants. Independent spectral/$hp$ calculations with the same Gaussian-regularized lid provide the reference fields. For a cavity of depth-to-width ratio $D/W=5$ at Reynolds numbers $\mathrm{Re}=100$, 250, 500, and 1000, evaluation on a common $121\times605$ grid gives interior relative velocity discrepancies of 5.130\%--7.850\%. Over the same cases, floor-region relative velocity discrepancies remain below 5\%, with absolute RMS discrepancies ranging from $1.255\times10^{-10}U$ to $2.332\times10^{-9}U$, where $U$ is the lid-velocity scale. In a separate $161\times801$ assessment at $\Rey=1000$, the refined workflow lowers interior velocity discrepancy from 5.624\% to 2.658\% and gauge-aligned pressure RMS discrepancy from $2.793\times10^{-3}$ to $1.167\times10^{-3}ρU^2$. The improvements compare accumulated training workflows and do not isolate regional sampling. Configuration rankings depend on both region and observable. These finite-budget comparisons establish where the retained workflows agree with the reference and where rotational-field discrepancies remain substantial.

AI.tldr: Data-free physics-informed neural networks with a hard-constrained streamfunction formulation were assessed for steady two-dimensional incompressible flow in a deep lid-driven cavity (D/W=5) at Re=100, 250, 500, and 1000 against independent spectral/hp reference calculations, showing moderate interior velocity discrepancies and smaller floor-region errors.
AI.motivation: Deep lid-driven cavities have strong motion beneath the lid but much weaker recirculation at depth, so agreement in bulk velocity alone is an incomplete assessment of a computed flow; the study therefore examines data-free PINNs for this flow configuration.
AI.method: The authors used data-free physics-informed neural networks for steady, two-dimensional incompressible cavity flow at depth-to-width ratio five and Reynolds numbers 100, 250, 500, and 1000. They combined an established hard-constrained streamfunction formulation with prescribed regional collocation, transferred initialization, and selected residual-scaling and envelope variants. Independent spectral/hp calculations using the same Gaussian-regularized lid provided reference fields. Evaluation used a common 121×605 grid and a separate 161×801 assessment at Re=1000.
AI.result: On the 121×605 grid, interior relative velocity discrepancies were 5.130%–7.850%; floor-region relative velocity discrepancies remained below 5%, with absolute RMS discrepancies from 1.255×10−10U to 2.332×10−9U. In the separate 161×801 assessment at Re=1000, the refined workflow reduced interior velocity discrepancy from 5.624% to 2.658% and gauge-aligned pressure RMS discrepancy from 2.793×10−3 to 1.167×10−3ρU². The improvements compare accumulated training workflows and do not isolate regional sampling; configuration rankings depended on both region and observable.
AI.conclusion: These finite-budget comparisons establish where the retained PINN workflows agree with the spectral/hp reference and where rotational-field discrepancies remain substantial; the abstract does not provide further conclusions beyond these comparisons.

title: Integrated Circular Polarisation Beam Shaper Based on Tilted Waveguide Bragg Gratings
summary: Scalable quantum platforms require optical systems that deliver well-defined polarisation without relying on macroscopic bulk optics or manual alignment, motivating chip-integrated approaches capable of shaping both the spatial mode and the polarisation of the emitted field. By developing a full three-dimensional analytical model of the scattering process together with numerical simulations to design and evaluate the emitted field, we show that tilted waveguide Bragg gratings can act as integrated polarisation beam shapers. We find that scattering two co-propagating, orthogonally polarised pumps on a single grating is fundamentally limited: waveguide birefringence and the difference in scattering efficiency prevent full polarisation control. We overcome this with an orthogonal superimposed-grating architecture in which two gratings driven independently by two pumps propagating perpendicular to each other succeed in generating any desired polarisation output apart from directions in a narrow spatial region. The approach provides a scalable, chip-integrated route to polarisation-engineered light delivery for quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: Tilted waveguide Bragg gratings can act as chip-integrated polarisation beam shapers, but a single grating driven by two co-propagating orthogonally polarised pumps cannot provide full polarisation control. An orthogonal superimposed-grating architecture driven by two perpendicular pumps overcomes this limitation and can generate nearly any desired polarisation, except for directions in a narrow spatial region.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum platforms need optical systems that deliver well-defined polarisation without macroscopic bulk optics or manual alignment, motivating chip-integrated approaches that can shape both the spatial mode and polarisation of the emitted field.
AI.method: The authors develop a full three-dimensional analytical model of the scattering process and use numerical simulations to design and evaluate the emitted field. They first assess tilted waveguide Bragg gratings driven by two co-propagating, orthogonally polarised pumps and then introduce an orthogonal superimposed-grating architecture in which two gratings are driven independently by two pumps propagating perpendicular to each other.
AI.result: Scattering two co-propagating, orthogonally polarised pumps on a single grating is fundamentally limited by waveguide birefringence and the difference in scattering efficiency, preventing full polarisation control. The orthogonal superimposed-grating architecture succeeds in generating any desired polarisation output apart from directions in a narrow spatial region.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides a scalable, chip-integrated route to polarisation-engineered light delivery for quantum technologies. The abstract does not provide quantitative performance metrics.

title: Diffusion model for fast alpha-particle transport in Magneto-Inertial Fusion plasmas
summary: A diffusion model is developed to describe fast alpha-particle transport and confinement in dense magnetized DT fusion plasmas, tailored to Magneto-Inertial Fusion conditions. The model, derived from the Fokker-Planck kinetic equation using the Chapman-Enskog approximation, includes dynamic Coulomb friction from electrons and ions. This approach improves upon earlier heuristic model [Liberman and Velikovich, J. Plasma Phys. 31, 369 (1984)], which, while valid in the ignition range near 5 keV, lacks accuracy at the higher temperatures ~20 keV required for high-gain Magnetized Liner Inertial Fusion (MagLIF). This paper provides explicit analytic formulas for all transport coefficients and characterizes the relationship between the alpha-particle pressure gradient and the associated Ampère force in magnetized plasmas, which are both relevant for MagLIF at high temperatures.

AI.tldr: A diffusion model is developed for fast alpha-particle transport and confinement in dense magnetized DT magneto-inertial fusion plasmas. Derived from the Fokker-Planck equation via the Chapman-Enskog approximation with dynamic Coulomb friction from electrons and ions, it provides explicit analytic transport coefficients and characterizes the alpha-pressure-gradient/Ampère-force relationship, improving on an earlier heuristic model that is inaccurate at the ~20 keV temperatures relevant to high-gain MagLIF.
AI.motivation: The earlier heuristic model is valid near the ~5 keV ignition range but lacks accuracy at the higher temperatures of about 20 keV required for high-gain Magnetized Liner Inertial Fusion (MagLIF), motivating a more accurate description of fast alpha-particle transport and confinement in dense magnetized DT plasmas.
AI.method: The authors derive a diffusion model from the Fokker-Planck kinetic equation using the Chapman-Enskog approximation, tailored to Magneto-Inertial Fusion conditions. The model includes dynamic Coulomb friction from electrons and ions, provides explicit analytic formulas for all transport coefficients, and characterizes the relationship between the alpha-particle pressure gradient and the associated Ampère force in magnetized plasmas.
AI.result: The paper presents the diffusion model, explicit analytic formulas for all transport coefficients, and a characterization of the alpha-particle pressure-gradient/Ampère-force relationship. It states improved accuracy over the earlier heuristic model at high temperatures relevant to MagLIF; no quantitative validation or performance results are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The diffusion model is intended for fast alpha-particle transport and confinement in dense magnetized DT Magneto-Inertial Fusion plasmas and is relevant to MagLIF at high temperatures. It improves upon the earlier heuristic model, but the abstract does not provide quantitative conclusions or experimental outcomes.

title: Hidden Phase Transition in Single-Polymer Stretching under Elongational Flow
summary: Using machine learning, we identify a second transition in polymer chain stretching driven by planar elongational flow, beyond the well-known coil-stretch transition. We achieve this by developing a conditional extension of Universal and Identifiable Dissipative Dynamics (UIDD) that jointly learns reduced stochastic dynamics from microscopic trajectories across flow strengths and yields the corresponding stationary nonequilibrium free energy landscapes. As the flow strength increases, the evolving landscape exhibits the expected coil-stretch transition, and then a previously unrecognized dynamical transition. In the latter, the stretched states persist, but the distribution along a folding coordinate becomes bimodal when conditioned on small end-to-end separation. title: Identifiability Limits of Reynolds-Stress Attribution in Localized Nonorthogonal Flow Representations
summary: Reynolds stress is assembled from correlations among velocity fluctuations; assigning it to named vortical structures additionally requires their velocity fields to be separable. Orthogonal Fourier and proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) regroupings of the same velocity remove this cancellation, showing that it follows from the local nonorthogonal organization rather than from the represented field alone. The morphology labels remain representation-dependent, but their physical consequence is direct: Reynolds stress in this local description is carried by coupled velocity fluctuations, not by additive component energies. title: Partially temporal coherent spatiotemporal Laguerre-Gaussian and its propagation dynamics
summary: Optical spatiotemporal vortices carrying transverse photonic orbital angular momentum have become an intense research topic in the recent study of structured light fields. Despite being mainly studied within the framework of fully coherent optical pulses, the complex topologies of the light field are also investigated with partially coherent light sources, offering an alternative pathway in applications. In this work, we theoretically and experimentally investigate partially temporally coherent spatiotemporal Laguerre-Gaussian (STLG) field with independently controllable radial and azimuthal indices. The spatiotemporal topological information, carried by the structured amplified spontaneous emission source, are well preserved in the presence of inherent instantaneous random temporal phase fluctuations. Under combined spatiotemporal astigmatism and group velocity dispersion, the partially temporally coherent STLG field can be converted into spatiotemporal Hermite-Gaussian (STHG) field. Both structures maintain their spatiotemporal characteristics after propagating through scattering media. Partially temporally coherent structured light fields may offer new insights into photonic topology and complex wave dynamics, with potential applications in high-fidelity optical communications and high-dimensional information processing in highly scattering environments.

title: A Macroscopic Model of Bipolar Corona Discharges for Ionic Thrusters Simulation
summary: Recent studies on Electro-Aero-Dynamic (EAD) thrusters have demonstrated that optimized, multi-stage, electrode arrangements can lead to substantial performance improvements. Existing models can be broadly classified into full plasma models, that account for the chemical kinetics in the ionization region and reduced models, that rely on simplifying assumptions, e.g. Kaptzov's hypothesis, to avoid the computation of the ionization region. Full plasma models, despite their accuracy, are computationally demanding, especially when coupled with the Navier-Stokes equations. Reduced models are computationally cheaper and therefore are well suited for the design process. Compact design EAD thrusters that use multiple stages with alternating polarity have recently appeared in literature. Such a configuration allows smaller inter-stage distances, because the emitter(s) of a stage cannot be ignited by the collector(s) of the previous one, as no voltage difference is applied between them. In this work, we introduce a reduced bipolar corona discharge model coupled to the Navier-Stokes equations. A numerical simulation code is implemented based on the high performance finite element deal.II library. Our model can successfully simulate multi-stage thrusters with alternating polarity configurations and automatically detect the ignition pattern, when a configuration with multiple emitters is considered. Validation is performed against previous experimental and numerical campaigns, demonstrating the good predictive capabilities of our model.

title: Distilling Large-Scale Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials to Predict Long-Timescale Electrolyte Transport Properties
summary: Accurately predicting the transport properties of liquid electrolytes is critical for next-generation battery design and requires force fields that are both quantum-mechanically accurate and fast enough for long-timescale simulation. Our distilled models run ~40x faster, reproduce teacher-predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days, rather than the months the teacher would require. Across a diverse set of sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions, establishing distillation as a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulations necessary for high-throughput electrolyte screening.

title: Kinetic linear stability theory for incompressible parallel shear flows with the full Boltzmann collision operator
summary: Modal and non-modal linear stability analysis of incompressible shear flows is performed for the first time by linearizing the Boltzmann equation and its full collision operator. In this kinetic linear stability theory (kLST) the hard-sphere operator and its BGK, ES-BGK and Shakhov relaxation models share the same discretization, so that their results can be compared directly. Written in the peculiar velocity about a Chapman-Enskog base state, the collision operators are independent of the cross-stream coordinate and are formed once. Summation-by-parts Legendre collocation, weak diffuse-reflection wall conditions and a moment-consistent velocity derivative yield an energy-stable discrete operator, verified to spectral accuracy by a manufactured solution. Numerical solution of the four-dimensional problem, comparable in size to a TriGlobal problem (Theofilis 2011), is made feasible by the fast spectral method of Gamba, Haack, Hauck and Hu (2017) for the full operator. Modal kLST uses matrix-free shift-invert Arnoldi iteration, preconditioned by an exact relaxation-model inverse. Non-modal kLST is based on an energy norm containing Chu's disturbance energy, a kinetic Reynolds-Orr equation identifying the mean shear as the only energy source. Transient growth and pseudospectra follow from the same preconditioned solves. For plane Couette and Poiseuille flows, the mixing layer and the Blasius boundary layer at Reynolds numbers 10^2-10^5, all four operators recover the Orr-Sommerfeld eigenvalues (Orszag 1971; Mack 1976) in the incompressible limit to a few parts in 10^7 for the models and 10^6 for the full operator. title: Non-Markovian quantum-emitter dynamics and bound-state formation in an Aubry--André--Harper photonic lattice
summary: In non-Markovian light-matter interactions, a spectrally structured bath can alter the evolution of a quantum emitter by modifying the vacuum fluctuations experienced by the emitter. This raises the question of how the localization transition and the associated multifractal critical modes induced by a quasiperiodic potential shape the emitter dynamics. We investigate this scenario in the single-excitation sector for a two-level quantum emitter coupled to an Aubry-André-Harper (AAH) photonic lattice. By externally tuning the strength of the quasiperiodic onsite modulation, the lattice is tuned from the extended to the localized regime through a critical point characterized by multifractal modes. Using modal analysis, we show that the quasiperiodic modulation reshapes the local density of states at the coupling site and thereby controls the effective spectral coupling between the emitter and the lattice. The transient dynamics depend strongly on the spatial and spectral overlap between the emitter and the lattice modes: extended modes below the critical modulation generally produce rapid depopulation, whereas critical and localized modes give rise to coherent back-action and persistent Rabi-like oscillations, with particularly pronounced behavior at the critical point. We further identify emitter-photon bound states whose formation is controlled by the quasiperiodic spectral structure of the bath and whose overlap with the initially excited state leads to partial long-time population trapping. These results establish a direct connection between quasiperiodic localization, non-Markovian dynamics, and emitter-photon bound-state formation.

title: Transition from laser Raman to Bernstein scattering in magnetized plasmas
summary: When a laser backscatters from an external perpendicular magnetic field, stimulated Raman scattering transitions to stimulated Bernstein scattering, which we show using kinetic theory and particle-in-cell simulations. For low field strengths, the magnetic field acts as an electron detrapping mechanism, suppressing nonlinear effects of Raman scattering. At stronger fields, when the electron cyclotron frequency ωce becomes non-negligible compared to the plasma frequency ωpe, the Raman resonance splits into discrete resonances mediated by electron Bernstein waves (EBWs). Raman scattering ceases to exist between the EBW resonances, which are narrower and stronger than the Raman resonance they replace. The replacement is sensitive to angle: When the magnetic field is away from perpendicular by an angle α {\gtrsim} ωce/ωpe, the damping of EBW resonances blends them back into a broad single Raman peak. Our results demonstrate that strong magnetic fields, either spontaneously generated or externally imposed in high-energy-density experiments, fundamentally change laser-plasma interactions in a way that has no analog in unmagnetized plasmas, with implications for field diagnostics, plasma photonics, and inertial confinement fusion.

AI.motivation: The study addresses how strong magnetic fields, either spontaneously generated or externally imposed in high-energy-density experiments, modify laser-plasma interactions, with relevance to field diagnostics, plasma photonics, and inertial confinement fusion.
AI.method: The authors use kinetic theory and particle-in-cell simulations to analyze laser backscattering from an external perpendicular magnetic field.
AI.result: At low field strengths, the magnetic field detraps electrons and suppresses nonlinear Raman effects. When the electron cyclotron frequency ωce is non-negligible relative to the plasma frequency ωpe, the Raman resonance splits into discrete electron-Bernstein-wave-mediated resonances that are narrower and stronger, with Raman scattering absent between them. title: Ten-loop fixed-dimension renormalization-group functions of the three-dimensional O(N) model from distributed GPU-accelerated parametric integration
comment: 30 pages, 2 figures. Code, data and reproducibility checks at https://github.com/PaoloRibeca/ReBar, archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23750242
summary: The renormalization-group functions $β$, $η$ and $ν$ of the three-dimensional $O(N)$ model in fixed dimension (massive zero-momentum scheme) were known to eighth order in the coupling. We extend them to tenth order, and $β$ to eleventh, for general $N$, which requires the two- and four-point functions to ten loops (1,593,254 graphs at the last order), and re-evaluate all lower orders. Through the Callan-Symanzik equation every coefficient follows from per-order sums that are linear in finite, zero-momentum $\bar R$-subtracted parametric integrals, one per graph, which we sample on GPUs by tropical Monte Carlo with densities adapted to the forest terms. The computation reproduces the known sums from two to seven loops within three standard deviations and agrees at ninth and tenth order, at lower precision, with an independent route through an intermediate scheme. The new coefficients have relative uncertainties of a few $10^{-5}$ or better, and the eighth-order coefficients of $η$ and $ν$ improve by factors of 120 and 4. The time needed to integrate an order to fixed relative precision grows by only 2.4-2.9 per loop from seven loops on, while the construction of the integrands still grows factorially and, at tenth order, costs more than the integration. Resummed, the tenth-order series give $ν=0.62997(51)$, $η=0.0333(18)$ and $ω=0.803(14)$ for $N=1$, against $0.62997097(12)$, $0.036297612(48)$ and $0.82968(23)$ from the conformal bootstrap; at $N=3$ the deviations grow, so that the uncertainty is now dominated by the resummation rather than by the coefficients. title: Modeling Broad-Frequency-Band Water-Wave Experiments with Generalizations of the Nonlinear Schrodinger Equation
summary: Waves generated by storms gradually disperse, forming swells that can travel thousands of kilometers across the ocean's surface. The evolution of deep-water swells, which are unaffected by the seafloor, can be modeled by the nonlinear Schrodinger (NLS) equation and its generalizations. These models typically assume that the wave trains are comprised of a narrow band of frequencies. We present measurements from a new series of laboratory experiments in which the broadbandedness is increased and show that generalizations of the NLS equation can accurately model these measurements.

AI.motivation: Deep-water swells are commonly modeled with the nonlinear Schrodinger equation and its generalizations, but these models typically assume narrow-band wave trains; the paper tests whether such models remain accurate when broadbandedness is increased.
AI.method: The authors conducted a new series of laboratory experiments on deep-water waves with increased broadbandedness and compared the measurements with predictions from generalizations of the nonlinear Schrodinger equation.
AI.result: Generalizations of the nonlinear Schrodinger equation accurately modeled the laboratory measurements. No quantitative error metrics or specific parameter ranges are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Generalized nonlinear Schrodinger models can accurately describe deep-water wave behavior in these more broadband laboratory conditions, supporting their use beyond the narrow-band assumption; broader applicability and quantitative limits are not specified in the abstract.

title: Symmetry-governed nonlinear metasurface simultaneously enhances circular dichroism, helicity purity, and Q-factor
summary: Circularly polarized light underpins a broad range of chiroptical and spin-selective photonic technologies, yet extending resonant chirality to nonlinear harmonic emission remains challenging. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a symmetry-governed mechanism that maps the maximal linear chirality of high-Q degenerate resonances onto the polarization of the generated harmonic. Preserved rotational symmetry protects modal degeneracy and polarization-selection rules, while broken mirror symmetries enable a strong chiroptical response. The metasurface thereby filters the pump polarization and purifies the handedness of the nonlinear output, simultaneously achieving third-harmonic circular dichroism of -0.98, a degree of circular polarization of 0.83, and an effective nonlinear Q-factor of 140. Importantly, the nonlinear emission preserves its handedness even under spatially depolarized excitation, demonstrating robustness to variations in the incident polarization state. These results establish complementary symmetry preservation and breaking as a deterministic route for transferring resonant chirality from linear to nonlinear optical responses, providing a general design principle for nonlinear chiral photonics.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates a symmetry-governed metasurface mechanism that transfers resonant linear chirality to nonlinear harmonic emission, achieving strong third-harmonic circular dichroism and robust output handedness.
AI.motivation: Circularly polarized light is important for chiroptical and spin-selective photonic technologies, but extending resonant chirality from linear to nonlinear harmonic emission remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors use a metasurface in which preserved rotational symmetry protects modal degeneracy and polarization-selection rules, while broken mirror symmetries enable a strong chiroptical response. This maps the maximal linear chirality of high-Q degenerate resonances onto the polarization of the generated harmonic, filtering the pump polarization and purifying the nonlinear output handedness.

AI.conclusion: Complementary symmetry preservation and breaking provide a deterministic route for transferring resonant chirality from linear to nonlinear optical responses and a general design principle for nonlinear chiral photonics.

title: Automated CR-39 pit detection for energy and angular characterization of laser-driven ion beams
comment: 7 pages, 8 figures; supplementary material included as an ancillary file. Published in AIP Advances. Code related to this work is available at https://github.com/wlin8633/CR39-pit-detector
summary: Accurate characterization of ion beams from sub-MeV to multi-MeV energies is essential for diagnostics in laser-driven ion acceleration and fusion research. CR-39 detectors are widely used to measure absolute ion yields, while ion energy and incidence angle can be inferred from etched-pit geometries.
